A pair of stocks, you rogue!
You'll end up in the stocks, you rascal!
Y'are a baggage; the Slys are no rogues; look in the chronicles: we / came in with Richard Conqueror. Therefore, paucas pallabris; let the / world slide. Sessa!
You're a slut. The Slys are no rascals: look in the history books, we came over with Richard the Conqueror. So, few words; let the world go by. Shut up!
You will not pay for the glasses you have burst?
So you won't pay for the glasses you've broken?
No, not a denier. Go by, Saint Jeronimy, go to thy cold bed and warm / thee.
No, not a penny. Get lost, Saint Jeronimy: go to your cold bed and warm yourself up.
I know my remedy; I must go fetch the third-borough.
I know what to do about this. I'll go and fetch the constable.
Third, or fourth, or fifth borough, I'll answer him by law. I'll not / budge an inch, boy: let him come, and kindly.
Constable, or fourth, or fifth constable, I'll answer him in court. I won't budge an inch, boy. Let him come, and welcome.

Huntsman, I charge thee, tender well my hounds; / Brach Merriman, the poor cur is emboss'd, / And couple Clowder with the deep-mouth'd brach. / Saw'st thou not, boy, how Silver made it good / At the hedge-corner, in the coldest fault? / I would not lose the dog for twenty pound.

Huntsman, I order you to look after my hounds well. Give Merriman a rest, the poor dog is foaming with exhaustion, and leash Clowder with the deep-voiced bitch. Did you see, boy, how Silver picked up the trail at the corner of the hedge, where the scent was coldest? I wouldn't lose that dog for twenty pounds.
Why, Bellman is as good as he, my lord; / He cried upon it at the merest loss, / And twice today pick'd out the dullest scent; / Trust me, I take him for the better dog.
Well, Bellman is as good as him, my lord. He bayed when the scent was completely lost, and twice today he found the faintest trail. Believe me, I think he's the better dog.
Thou art a fool: if Echo were as fleet, / I would esteem him worth a dozen such. / But sup them well, and look unto them all; / Tomorrow I intend to hunt again.
You're a fool. If Echo were as fast, I'd value him at a dozen like Bellman. But feed them well and look after them all. I mean to hunt again tomorrow.
[Sees Sly] What's here? One dead, or drunk? / See, doth he breathe?
What's this? Is he dead, or drunk? See if he's breathing.
He breathes, my lord. Were he not warm'd with ale, / This were a bed but cold to sleep so soundly.
He's breathing, my lord. If he weren't warmed up with ale, this would be a cold bed to sleep so soundly in.

O monstrous beast! how like a swine he lies! / Grim death, how foul and loathsome is thine image! / Sirs, I will practise on this drunken man. / What think you, if he were convey'd to bed, / Wrapp'd in sweet clothes, rings put upon his fingers, / A most delicious banquet by his bed, / And brave attendants near him when he wakes, / Would not the beggar then forget himself?

What a disgusting beast! He lies there like a pig! Death, how ugly and loathsome your likeness is! Gentlemen, I'm going to play a trick on this drunk. What do you think: if he were carried to bed, wrapped in perfumed clothes, with rings put on his fingers, a delicious banquet by his bed and finely dressed servants around him when he wakes, wouldn't the beggar forget who he is?
Believe me, lord, I think he cannot choose.
Believe me, my lord, I don't think he could help it.
It would seem strange unto him when he wak'd.
It would seem strange to him when he woke up.

Even as a flattering dream or worthless fancy. / Then take him up, and manage well the jest. / Carry him gently to my fairest chamber, / And hang it round with all my wanton pictures; / Balm his foul head in warm distilled waters, / And burn sweet wood to make the lodging sweet. / Procure me music ready when he wakes, / To make a dulcet and a heavenly sound; / And if he chance to speak, be ready straight, / And with a low submissive reverence / Say 'What is it your honour will command?' / Let one attend him with a silver basin / Full of rose-water and bestrew'd with flowers; / Another bear the ewer, the third a diaper, / And say 'Will't please your lordship cool your hands?' / Someone be ready with a costly suit, / And ask him what apparel he will wear; / Another tell him of his hounds and horse, / And that his lady mourns at his disease. / Persuade him that he hath been lunatic; / And, when he says he is—say that he dreams, / For he is nothing but a mighty lord. / This do, and do it kindly, gentle sirs; / It will be pastime passing excellent, / If it be husbanded with modesty.

Just like a flattering dream or an empty fantasy. Then pick him up and carry the joke off well. Carry him gently to my finest bedroom and hang it all round with my sexiest pictures. Bathe his filthy head in warm perfumed water and burn sweet-smelling wood to scent the room. Have music ready for when he wakes, to make a sweet and heavenly sound. And if he happens to speak, be ready at once to bow low and humbly and say, "What does your honour command?" Let one of you wait on him with a silver basin full of rose-water scattered with flowers, another carry the jug, a third a towel, and say, "Would your lordship like to cool your hands?" Have someone ready with an expensive suit of clothes to ask him what he wants to wear. Have another tell him about his hounds and horse, and that his lady is grieving over his illness. Convince him he's been mad, and when he says he is himself, say he's dreaming, because he is nothing other than a mighty lord. Do this, and do it naturally, good sirs. It'll be wonderful entertainment if it's handled with restraint.
My lord, I warrant you we will play our part, / As he shall think by our true diligence, / He is no less than what we say he is.
My lord, I promise you we'll play our part so well that he'll think, from our careful service, that he's exactly what we say he is.
Take him up gently, and to bed with him, / And each one to his office when he wakes.
Pick him up gently and put him to bed, and each of you take up your job when he wakes.
Sirrah, go see what trumpet 'tis that sounds.
You there, go and see what that trumpet is.
Belike some noble gentleman that means, / Travelling some journey, to repose him here.
It's probably some nobleman on a journey who wants to rest here.
An it please your honour, players / That offer service to your lordship.
If it please your honour, some actors, who offer their services to your lordship.
Do you intend to stay with me tonight?
Do you mean to stay with me tonight?
So please your lordship to accept our duty.
If your lordship will accept our services.

With all my heart. This fellow I remember / Since once he play'd a farmer's eldest son; / 'Twas where you woo'd the gentlewoman so well. / I have forgot your name; but, sure, that part / Was aptly fitted and naturally perform'd.

With all my heart. I remember this man playing a farmer's eldest son once. It was the play where you wooed the lady so well. I've forgotten your name, but that part was well suited to you and naturally played.
I think 'twas Soto that your honour means.
I think your honour means Soto.

'Tis very true; thou didst it excellent. / Well, you are come to me in happy time, / The rather for I have some sport in hand / Wherein your cunning can assist me much. / There is a lord will hear you play tonight; / But I am doubtful of your modesties, / Lest, over-eying of his odd behaviour,— / For yet his honour never heard a play,— / You break into some merry passion / And so offend him; for I tell you, sirs, / If you should smile, he grows impatient.

That's right; you were excellent in it. Well, you've come at just the right moment, especially since I have some fun planned that your skill can help with a great deal. There is a lord who will hear you perform tonight. But I'm worried about your self-control. If you catch sight of his odd behaviour (because his honour has never seen a play), you might burst out laughing and offend him. I warn you, sirs, if you smile he'll lose his temper.
Fear not, my lord; we can contain ourselves, / Were he the veriest antick in the world.
Don't worry, my lord. We can control ourselves, even if he were the biggest clown in the world.
Go, sirrah, take them to the buttery, / And give them friendly welcome everyone: / Let them want nothing that my house affords.
Go on, you, take them to the pantry and give them all a friendly welcome. Let them have anything my house can give.

Sirrah, go you to Barthol'mew my page, / And see him dress'd in all suits like a lady; / That done, conduct him to the drunkard's chamber, / And call him 'madam,' do him obeisance. / Tell him from me—as he will win my love,— / He bear himself with honourable action, / Such as he hath observ'd in noble ladies / Unto their lords, by them accomplished; / Such duty to the drunkard let him do, / With soft low tongue and lowly courtesy, / And say 'What is't your honour will command, / Wherein your lady and your humble wife / May show her duty and make known her love?' / And then with kind embracements, tempting kisses, / And with declining head into his bosom, / Bid him shed tears, as being overjoy'd / To see her noble lord restor'd to health, / Who for this seven years hath esteemed him / No better than a poor and loathsome beggar. / And if the boy have not a woman's gift / To rain a shower of commanded tears, / An onion will do well for such a shift, / Which, in a napkin being close convey'd, / Shall in despite enforce a watery eye. / See this dispatch'd with all the haste thou canst; / Anon I'll give thee more instructions.

You there, go to my page Bartholomew and have him dressed in every detail like a lady. When that's done, take him to the drunkard's room, call him "madam" and bow to him. Tell him from me that, if he wants my favour, he must behave with dignity, the way he has seen noble ladies behave towards their husbands. Let him show the drunkard that kind of respect, with a soft, low voice and humble curtsies, and say, "What does your honour command, so that your lady and humble wife can show her duty and her love?" And then, with warm hugs and tempting kisses, laying his head on his chest, he must shed tears, as if overjoyed to see his noble husband restored to health, after seven years of thinking himself nothing but a poor, disgusting beggar. And if the boy can't cry on command the way women can, an onion will do the trick: wrapped up secretly in a handkerchief, it will force his eyes to water whether he likes it or not. See this done as fast as you can. I'll give you more instructions soon.

I know the boy will well usurp the grace, / Voice, gait, and action of a gentlewoman; / I long to hear him call the drunkard husband; / And how my men will stay themselves from laughter / When they do homage to this simple peasant. / I'll in to counsel them; haply my presence / May well abate the over-merry spleen, / Which otherwise would grow into extremes.

I know the boy will copy the grace, voice, walk and manner of a lady well. I can't wait to hear him call the drunkard "husband", and to see how my men keep from laughing when they bow to this simple peasant. I'll go in and advise them. Perhaps my being there will hold back their high spirits, which might otherwise get out of hand.
For God's sake! a pot of small ale.
For God's sake, a pot of weak ale!
Will't please your lordship drink a cup of sack?
Would your lordship like a cup of sherry?
Will't please your honour taste of these conserves?
Would your honour like to taste these candied fruits?
What raiment will your honour wear today?
What clothes will your honour wear today?

I am Christophero Sly; call not me honour nor lordship. I ne'er drank / sack in my life; and if you give me any conserves, give me conserves of / beef. Ne'er ask me what raiment I'll wear, for I have no more doublets / than backs, no more stockings than legs, nor no more shoes than feet: / nay, sometime more feet than shoes, or such shoes as my toes look / through the over-leather.

I'm Christopher Sly. Don't call me "honour" or "lordship". I've never drunk sherry in my life, and if you give me any preserves, give me preserved beef. Don't ever ask me what clothes I'll wear, because I've no more jackets than backs, no more stockings than legs, and no more shoes than feet. In fact, sometimes I've more feet than shoes, or shoes so worn that my toes stick out through the leather.
Heaven cease this idle humour in your honour! / O, that a mighty man of such descent, / Of such possessions, and so high esteem, / Should be infused with so foul a spirit!
Heaven put an end to this silly fancy of your honour's! Oh, that a mighty man of such noble family, with such property and such high reputation, should be possessed by so foul a spirit!

What! would you make me mad? Am not I Christopher Sly, old Sly's son of / Burton-heath; by birth a pedlar, by education a cardmaker, by / transmutation a bear-herd, and now by present profession a tinker? Ask / Marian Hacket, the fat ale-wife of Wincot, if she know me not: if she / say I am not fourteen pence on the score for sheer ale, score me up for / the lyingest knave in Christendom. What! I am not bestraught. Here's—

What, are you trying to drive me mad? Aren't I Christopher Sly, old Sly's son from Barton-on-the-Heath, a pedlar by birth, a maker of wool-combs by training, then a bear-keeper by a change of trade, and now a tinker by profession? Ask Marian Hacket, the fat alewife of Wincot, if she doesn't know me. If she says I don't owe her fourteen pence on my tab for pure ale, put me down as the biggest liar in Christendom. What! I'm not out of my mind. Here's...
O! this it is that makes your lady mourn.
Oh, this is what makes your lady grieve!
O! this is it that makes your servants droop.
Oh, this is what makes your servants so downcast!

Hence comes it that your kindred shuns your house, / As beaten hence by your strange lunacy. / O noble lord, bethink thee of thy birth, / Call home thy ancient thoughts from banishment, / And banish hence these abject lowly dreams. / Look how thy servants do attend on thee, / Each in his office ready at thy beck: / Wilt thou have music? Hark! Apollo plays,

This is why your relatives keep away from your house, as if driven off by your strange madness. Oh noble lord, think of your noble birth. Call your old thoughts home from exile, and banish these low, wretched dreams. Look how your servants wait on you, each ready to do his job at your nod. Would you like music? Listen! Apollo is playing,

And twenty caged nightingales do sing: / Or wilt thou sleep? We'll have thee to a couch / Softer and sweeter than the lustful bed / On purpose trimm'd up for Semiramis. / Say thou wilt walk: we will bestrew the ground: / Or wilt thou ride? Thy horses shall be trapp'd, / Their harness studded all with gold and pearl. / Dost thou love hawking? Thou hast hawks will soar / Above the morning lark: or wilt thou hunt? / Thy hounds shall make the welkin answer them / And fetch shrill echoes from the hollow earth.

and twenty caged nightingales are singing. Or would you like to sleep? We'll take you to a couch softer and sweeter than the bed specially made up for the lustful queen Semiramis. Say you'd like to walk, and we'll strew the ground with flowers. Or would you like to ride? Your horses will be decked out with harness studded with gold and pearl. Do you love hawking? You have hawks that will fly higher than the morning lark. Or would you like to hunt? Your hounds will make the sky ring and draw shrill echoes from the hollow earth.
Say thou wilt course; thy greyhounds are as swift / As breathed stags; ay, fleeter than the roe.
Say you'd like to go coursing: your greyhounds are as swift as stags in full stride, yes, faster than a deer.

Dost thou love pictures? We will fetch thee straight / Adonis painted by a running brook, / And Cytherea all in sedges hid, / Which seem to move and wanton with her breath / Even as the waving sedges play with wind.

Do you love paintings? We'll bring you at once Adonis painted beside a running stream, and Venus hidden in the reeds, which seem to move and flirt with her breath, just as the waving reeds play in the wind.
We'll show thee Io as she was a maid / And how she was beguiled and surpris'd, / As lively painted as the deed was done.
We'll show you Io as she was when still a girl, and how she was tricked and taken by surprise, painted as vividly as if it were happening.
Or Daphne roaming through a thorny wood, / Scratching her legs, that one shall swear she bleeds / And at that sight shall sad Apollo weep, / So workmanly the blood and tears are drawn.
Or Daphne running through a thorny wood, scratching her legs so that you'd swear she was bleeding, and at the sight sad Apollo weeps, so skilfully are the blood and tears painted.
Thou art a lord, and nothing but a lord: / Thou hast a lady far more beautiful / Than any woman in this waning age.
You're a lord, and nothing but a lord. You have a lady far more beautiful than any woman in this declining age.
And, till the tears that she hath shed for thee / Like envious floods o'er-run her lovely face, / She was the fairest creature in the world; / And yet she is inferior to none.
And until the tears she has shed for you flowed like spiteful floods over her lovely face, she was the most beautiful creature in the world. And even now she's second to none.

Am I a lord? and have I such a lady? / Or do I dream? Or have I dream'd till now? / I do not sleep: I see, I hear, I speak; / I smell sweet savours, and I feel soft things: / Upon my life, I am a lord indeed; / And not a tinker, nor Christophero Sly. / Well, bring our lady hither to our sight; / And once again, a pot o' the smallest ale.

Am I a lord? And do I have a lady like that? Or am I dreaming? Or have I been dreaming until now? I'm not asleep: I can see, hear and speak. I can smell sweet smells and feel soft things. Upon my life, I really am a lord, and not a tinker, or Christopher Sly. Well, bring our lady here for us to see. And once again, a pot of the weakest ale.
Will't please your mightiness to wash your hands?
Would your mightiness like to wash your hands?
O, how we joy to see your wit restor'd! / O, that once more you knew but what you are! / These fifteen years you have been in a dream, / Or, when you wak'd, so wak'd as if you slept.
Oh, how glad we are to see your mind restored! Oh, if only you knew again who you are! You've been in a dream for fifteen years, or when you were awake, it was as if you were asleep.
These fifteen years! by my fay, a goodly nap. / But did I never speak of all that time?
Fifteen years! By my faith, that's a good long nap. But did I never speak in all that time?

O! yes, my lord, but very idle words; / For though you lay here in this goodly chamber, / Yet would you say ye were beaten out of door, / And rail upon the hostess of the house, / And say you would present her at the leet, / Because she brought stone jugs and no seal'd quarts. / Sometimes you would call out for Cicely Hacket.

Oh yes, my lord, but nothing but nonsense. Though you were lying here in this fine room, you'd say you'd been thrown out of doors, and you'd rant at the landlady of the inn and say you'd take her to the local court because she served drinks in stone jugs, not in proper measured quarts. Sometimes you'd call out for Cicely Hacket.
Ay, the woman's maid of the house.
Yes, the landlady's maid at the inn.

Why, sir, you know no house nor no such maid, / Nor no such men as you have reckon'd up, / As Stephen Sly, and old John Naps of Greece, / And Peter Turph, and Henry Pimpernell; / And twenty more such names and men as these, / Which never were, nor no man ever saw.

Why, sir, you don't know any such inn or any such maid, or any of the men you've listed, like Stephen Sly, old John Naps of Greece, Peter Turph and Henry Pimpernell, and twenty more names and men like them, who never existed and nobody ever saw.
Now, Lord be thanked for my good amends!
Well, thank the Lord for my recovery!
I thank thee; thou shalt not lose by it.
Thank you. You won't lose by it.
Marry, I fare well; for here is cheer enough. / Where is my wife?
Well, I'm doing fine, because there's plenty of good food and drink here. Where's my wife?
Here, noble lord: what is thy will with her?
Here, noble lord. What do you want with her?
Are you my wife, and will not call me husband? / My men should call me lord: I am your goodman.
Are you my wife, and you won't call me husband? My servants should call me "lord". To you I'm your husband.
My husband and my lord, my lord and husband; / I am your wife in all obedience.
My husband and my lord, my lord and husband: I am your wife, and wholly obedient.
I know it well. What must I call her?
I know that. What should I call her?
Madam, and nothing else; so lords call ladies.
Madam, and nothing else. That's what lords call ladies.
Madam wife, they say that I have dream'd / And slept above some fifteen year or more.
Madam wife, they say I've been dreaming and asleep for fifteen years or more.
Ay, and the time seems thirty unto me, / Being all this time abandon'd from your bed.
Yes, and it seems like thirty to me, shut out from your bed all this time.
'Tis much. Servants, leave me and her alone. / Madam, undress you, and come now to bed.
That's a long time. Servants, leave me alone with her. Madam, get undressed and come to bed now.

Thrice noble lord, let me entreat of you / To pardon me yet for a night or two; / Or, if not so, until the sun be set: / For your physicians have expressly charg'd, / In peril to incur your former malady, / That I should yet absent me from your bed: / I hope this reason stands for my excuse.

Most noble lord, let me beg you to excuse me for another night or two, or if not that, until sunset. Your doctors have given strict orders that I should keep away from your bed for now, or you risk falling back into your old illness. I hope this reason will excuse me.
Ay, it stands so that I may hardly tarry so long; but I would be loath / to fall into my dreams again: I will therefore tarry in despite of the / flesh and the blood.
Yes, well, it's standing up so that I can hardly wait that long. But I'd hate to fall back into my dreams. So I'll wait, in spite of my flesh and blood.

Your honour's players, hearing your amendment, / Are come to play a pleasant comedy; / For so your doctors hold it very meet, / Seeing too much sadness hath congeal'd your blood, / And melancholy is the nurse of frenzy: / Therefore they thought it good you hear a play, / And frame your mind to mirth and merriment, / Which bars a thousand harms and lengthens life.

Your honour's actors, hearing that you've recovered, have come to perform a pleasant comedy. Your doctors think it a very good idea, since too much sadness has thickened your blood, and melancholy feeds madness. So they thought it best that you should watch a play and turn your mind to mirth and fun, which prevents a thousand harms and lengthens life.
Marry, I will; let them play it. Is not a commonty a Christmas gambold / or a tumbling-trick?
Well, I will. Let them perform it. Isn't a "commonty" a Christmas romp or an acrobatic trick?
No, my good lord; it is more pleasing stuff.
No, my good lord. It's more pleasing stuff.
It is a kind of history.
Well, we'll see't. Come, madam wife, sit by my side and let the world / slip: we shall ne'er be younger.
Well, we'll see it. Come, madam wife, sit by my side and let the world go by. We'll never be younger.

Tranio, since for the great desire I had / To see fair Padua, nursery of arts, / I am arriv'd for fruitful Lombardy, / The pleasant garden of great Italy, / And by my father's love and leave am arm'd / With his good will and thy good company, / My trusty servant well approv'd in all, / Here let us breathe, and haply institute / A course of learning and ingenious studies. / Pisa, renowned for grave citizens, / Gave me my being and my father first, / A merchant of great traffic through the world, / Vincentio, come of the Bentivolii. / Vincentio's son, brought up in Florence, / It shall become to serve all hopes conceiv'd, / To deck his fortune with his virtuous deeds: / And therefore, Tranio, for the time I study, / Virtue and that part of philosophy / Will I apply that treats of happiness / By virtue specially to be achiev'd. / Tell me thy mind; for I have Pisa left / And am to Padua come as he that leaves / A shallow plash to plunge him in the deep, / And with satiety seeks to quench his thirst.

Tranio, because I longed so much to see beautiful Padua, the nursery of the arts, I have arrived in fertile Lombardy, the pleasant garden of great Italy. My father's love and permission have equipped me with his goodwill and your good company, my trusty servant, proven in everything. So let's settle here and perhaps begin a course of learning and clever studies. Pisa, famous for its serious citizens, gave me my life, and gave life first to my father, Vincentio, a merchant who trades all over the world and comes of the Bentivolii family. It's right that Vincentio's son, brought up in Florence, should fulfil all the hopes people have of him and add good deeds to his good fortune. So, Tranio, while I'm studying, I'll apply myself to virtue and to the part of philosophy that deals with happiness achieved through virtue. Tell me what you think, because I have left Pisa and come to Padua like a man who leaves a shallow puddle to plunge into the deep sea, and seeks to drink his fill.

Mi perdonato, gentle master mine; / I am in all affected as yourself; / Glad that you thus continue your resolve / To suck the sweets of sweet philosophy. / Only, good master, while we do admire / This virtue and this moral discipline, / Let's be no stoics nor no stocks, I pray; / Or so devote to Aristotle's checks / As Ovid be an outcast quite abjur'd. / Balk logic with acquaintance that you have, / And practise rhetoric in your common talk; / Music and poesy use to quicken you; / The mathematics and the metaphysics, / Fall to them as you find your stomach serves you: / No profit grows where is no pleasure ta'en; / In brief, sir, study what you most affect.

Pardon me, my good master. I feel exactly the same as you, and I'm glad you're keeping to your resolve to suck the sweets of sweet philosophy. Only, good master, while we admire this virtue and moral discipline, let's not be stoics, or wooden blocks, I beg you, or be so devoted to Aristotle's rules that we give up Ovid's poems of love entirely. Argue logic with the friends you have, and practise rhetoric in everyday conversation. Use music and poetry to liven you up. As for mathematics and metaphysics, tackle them when you have the appetite for them. You get nothing out of what you don't enjoy. In short, sir, study what you like best.

Gramercies, Tranio, well dost thou advise. / If, Biondello, thou wert come ashore, / We could at once put us in readiness, / And take a lodging fit to entertain / Such friends as time in Padua shall beget. / But stay awhile; what company is this?

Thank you, Tranio; that's good advice. If only Biondello had come ashore, we could get ready at once and take lodgings fit to entertain the friends we'll make in time here in Padua. But wait a moment: who are these people?
Master, some show to welcome us to town.
Master, it's some show to welcome us to town.

Gentlemen, importune me no farther, / For how I firmly am resolv'd you know; / That is, not to bestow my youngest daughter / Before I have a husband for the elder. / If either of you both love Katherina, / Because I know you well and love you well, / Leave shall you have to court her at your pleasure.

Gentlemen, stop pestering me. You know how firmly I've made up my mind: I won't let my youngest daughter marry before I have a husband for the elder one. If either of you loves Katherina, then, because I know you well and like you, you have my permission to court her as you please.
To cart her rather: she's too rough for me. / There, there, Hortensio, will you any wife?
Cart her through the streets, more like: she's too rough for me. There you are, Hortensio: do you want a wife?
[To Baptista] I pray you, sir, is it your will / To make a stale of me amongst these mates?
I ask you, sir, do you mean to make me a laughing stock among these low types?
Mates, maid! How mean you that? No mates for you, / Unless you were of gentler, milder mould.
Low types, girl? What do you mean by that? There'll be no mates for you, unless you were made of gentler, milder stuff.

I' faith, sir, you shall never need to fear; / I wis it is not half way to her heart; / But if it were, doubt not her care should be / To comb your noddle with a three-legg'd stool, / And paint your face, and use you like a fool.

Really, sir, you'll never need to worry. Marrying you isn't half way to her heart. But if it were, you can be sure she'd take care to comb your head with a three-legged stool, paint your face with blood and treat you like a fool.
From all such devils, good Lord deliver us!
From all such devils, good Lord deliver us!
Husht, master! Here's some good pastime toward: / That wench is stark mad or wonderful froward.
Hush, master! There's some good entertainment coming. That girl is either stark mad or amazingly stubborn.
But in the other's silence do I see / Maid's mild behaviour and sobriety. / Peace, Tranio!
But in the other one's silence I see a young woman's mild behaviour and modesty. Quiet, Tranio!
Well said, master; mum! and gaze your fill.
Well said, master. Mum's the word, and gaze your fill.
Gentlemen, that I may soon make good / What I have said,—Bianca, get you in: / And let it not displease thee, good Bianca, / For I will love thee ne'er the less, my girl.
Gentlemen, so that I can quickly carry out what I've said: Bianca, go inside. And don't be upset, good Bianca, because I won't love you any less, my girl.
A pretty peat! it is best put finger in the eye, and she knew why.
The pretty pet! She'd better poke her finger in her eye to make herself cry, if only she could think of a reason.
Sister, content you in my discontent. / Sir, to your pleasure humbly I subscribe: / My books and instruments shall be my company, / On them to look, and practise by myself.
Sister, be happy that I'm unhappy. Sir, I humbly accept your wishes. My books and instruments will be my company; I'll study them and practise by myself.
Hark, Tranio! thou mayst hear Minerva speak.
Listen, Tranio! You can hear the goddess of wisdom speak.
Signior Baptista, will you be so strange? / Sorry am I that our good will effects / Bianca's grief.
Signior Baptista, will you be so unfriendly? I'm sorry that our good intentions cause Bianca grief.
Why will you mew her up, / Signior Baptista, for this fiend of hell, / And make her bear the penance of her tongue?
Why will you shut her up like a caged hawk, Signior Baptista, because of this fiend from hell, and make her pay the price for her sister's tongue?
Gentlemen, content ye; I am resolv'd. / Go in, Bianca.
Gentlemen, be satisfied. My mind is made up. Go in, Bianca.

And for I know she taketh most delight / In music, instruments, and poetry, / Schoolmasters will I keep within my house / Fit to instruct her youth. If you, Hortensio, / Or, Signior Gremio, you, know any such, / Prefer them hither; for to cunning men / I will be very kind, and liberal / To mine own children in good bringing up; / And so, farewell. Katherina, you may stay; / For I have more to commune with Bianca.

And because I know she takes most delight in music, instruments and poetry, I'll keep schoolmasters in my house fit to teach her while she's young. If you, Hortensio, or you, Signior Gremio, know any such men, recommend them to me. I'll be very generous to skilled men, and generous in giving my own children a good upbringing. And so, goodbye. Katherina, you can stay, because I have more to talk about with Bianca.
Why, and I trust I may go too, may I not? What! shall I be appointed / hours, as though, belike, I knew not what to take and what to leave? / Ha!
Why, I suppose I can go too, can't I? What, am I to be given a timetable, as though I didn't know what to take and what to leave? Ha!

You may go to the devil's dam: your gifts are so good here's none will / hold you. Their love is not so great, Hortensio, but we may blow our / nails together, and fast it fairly out; our cake's dough on both sides. / Farewell: yet, for the love I bear my sweet Bianca, if I can by any / means light on a fit man to teach her that wherein she delights, I will / wish him to her father.

You can go to the devil's mother. Your qualities are so good that nobody here wants to keep you. Their love isn't so great, Hortensio, that we can't blow on our nails and patiently wait it out. Our cake is still dough on both sides: neither of us has succeeded. Goodbye. Still, for the love I have for my sweet Bianca, if I can by any means find a suitable man to teach her the things she enjoys, I'll recommend him to her father.

So will I, Signior Gremio: but a word, I pray. Though the nature of our / quarrel yet never brooked parle, know now, upon advice, it toucheth us / both,—that we may yet again have access to our fair mistress, and be / happy rivals in Bianca's love,—to labour and effect one thing / specially.

So will I, Signior Gremio. But a word, please. Although our rivalry has never allowed us to talk till now, now that I've thought about it, it concerns us both, if we're ever to get back to our lovely mistress and be happy rivals for Bianca's love, to work together to achieve one thing above all.
Marry, sir, to get a husband for her sister.
Why, sir, to get a husband for her sister.
A husband! A devil, you mean.
I say, a devil. Thinkest thou, Hortensio, though her father be very / rich, any man is so very a fool to be married to hell?
And I say a devil. Do you really think, Hortensio, that even though her father is very rich, any man is such a fool as to marry hell?

Tush, Gremio! Though it pass your patience and mine to endure her loud / alarums, why, man, there be good fellows in the world, and a man could / light on them, would take her with all faults, and money enough.

Nonsense, Gremio! Though it's beyond your patience and mine to put up with her noisy outbursts, why, man, there are good fellows in the world, if you could only find them, who'd take her with all her faults, if there's enough money.
I cannot tell; but I had as lief take her dowry with this condition: to / be whipp'd at the high cross every morning.
I don't know. I'd as soon take her dowry on this condition: to be whipped at the market cross every morning.

Faith, as you say, there's small choice in rotten apples. But come; / since this bar in law makes us friends, it shall be so far forth / friendly maintained, till by helping Baptista's eldest daughter to a / husband, we set his youngest free for a husband, and then have to't / afresh. Sweet Bianca! Happy man be his dole! He that runs fastest gets / the ring. How say you, Signior Gremio?

Well, as you say, there's not much to choose between rotten apples. But come: since this obstacle makes us friends, let's stay friendly until, by finding Baptista's eldest daughter a husband, we free his youngest to have a husband, and then we'll go at it again. Sweet Bianca! Good luck to the winner! The fastest runner gets the prize. What do you say, Signior Gremio?
I am agreed; and would I had given him the best horse in Padua to begin / his wooing, that would thoroughly woo her, wed her, and bed her, and / rid the house of her. Come on.
I agree. And I'd give the best horse in Padua to any man who'd start wooing her, who'd woo her thoroughly, marry her, bed her and get her out of the house. Come on.
I pray, sir, tell me, is it possible / That love should of a sudden take such hold?
Tell me, sir, please, is it possible for love to take such a hold so suddenly?

O Tranio! till I found it to be true, / I never thought it possible or likely; / But see, while idly I stood looking on, / I found the effect of love in idleness; / And now in plainness do confess to thee, / That art to me as secret and as dear / As Anna to the Queen of Carthage was, / Tranio, I burn, I pine, I perish, Tranio, / If I achieve not this young modest girl. / Counsel me, Tranio, for I know thou canst: / Assist me, Tranio, for I know thou wilt.

Oh, Tranio! Until I found it was true, I never thought it possible or likely. But look: while I stood idly watching, I felt love-in-idleness work on me. And now I'll confess plainly to you, who are as trusted and dear to me as Anna was to her sister Dido, Queen of Carthage: Tranio, I burn, I pine, I'll die, Tranio, if I don't win this modest young girl. Advise me, Tranio, because I know you can. Help me, Tranio, because I know you will.
Master, it is no time to chide you now; / Affection is not rated from the heart: / If love have touch'd you, nought remains but so: / Redime te captum quam queas minimo.

Master, this is no time to scold you. You can't drive love out of the heart by telling it off. If love has struck you, there's only one thing to do: buy yourself free from captivity as cheaply as you can.
Gramercies, lad; go forward; this contents; / The rest will comfort, for thy counsel's sound.
Thanks, lad. Go on: this is helpful. The rest will comfort me, because your advice is sound.
Master, you look'd so longly on the maid. / Perhaps you mark'd not what's the pith of all.
Master, you gazed so long at the girl that perhaps you didn't notice the main point of it all.
O, yes, I saw sweet beauty in her face, / Such as the daughter of Agenor had, / That made great Jove to humble him to her hand, / When with his knees he kiss'd the Cretan strand.
Oh yes, I saw sweet beauty in her face, like the beauty of Europa, Agenor's daughter, which made mighty Jove humble himself to her when he knelt on the shore of Crete.
Saw you no more? mark'd you not how her sister / Began to scold and raise up such a storm / That mortal ears might hardly endure the din?
Didn't you see anything else? Didn't you notice how her sister began to scold and raised such a storm that human ears could hardly bear the noise?
Tranio, I saw her coral lips to move, / And with her breath she did perfume the air; / Sacred and sweet was all I saw in her.
Tranio, I saw her coral lips move, and her breath perfumed the air. Everything I saw in her was holy and sweet.

Nay, then, 'tis time to stir him from his trance. / I pray, awake, sir: if you love the maid, / Bend thoughts and wits to achieve her. Thus it stands: / Her elder sister is so curst and shrewd, / That till the father rid his hands of her, / Master, your love must live a maid at home; / And therefore has he closely mew'd her up, / Because she will not be annoy'd with suitors.

Well, then, it's time to wake him from his trance. Please wake up, sir. If you love the girl, turn your thoughts and wits to winning her. This is how things stand: her elder sister is so bad-tempered and shrewish that until her father gets her off his hands, master, your love must stay home unmarried. And so he's shut her away, so she won't be bothered by suitors.
Ah, Tranio, what a cruel father's he! / But art thou not advis'd he took some care / To get her cunning schoolmasters to instruct her?
Ah, Tranio, what a cruel father he is! But did you notice that he's taking care to find skilled schoolmasters to teach her?
Ay, marry, am I, sir, and now 'tis plotted.
Yes, indeed I did, sir, and now I've got a plan.
Master, for my hand, / Both our inventions meet and jump in one.
Master, I'll bet both our ideas are exactly the same.
You will be schoolmaster, / And undertake the teaching of the maid: / That's your device.
You'll be a schoolmaster and take on teaching the girl. That's your plan.
It is: may it be done?
It is. Can it be done?
Not possible; for who shall bear your part / And be in Padua here Vincentio's son; / Keep house and ply his book, welcome his friends; / Visit his countrymen, and banquet them?
Impossible. Who'll play your part and be Vincentio's son here in Padua: keep house, study his books, welcome his friends, visit his fellow citizens and give them dinners?

Basta, content thee, for I have it full. / We have not yet been seen in any house, / Nor can we be distinguish'd by our faces / For man or master: then it follows thus: / Thou shalt be master, Tranio, in my stead, / Keep house and port and servants, as I should; / I will some other be; some Florentine, / Some Neapolitan, or meaner man of Pisa. / 'Tis hatch'd, and shall be so: Tranio, at once / Uncase thee; take my colour'd hat and cloak. / When Biondello comes, he waits on thee; / But I will charm him first to keep his tongue.

Enough, don't worry, because I've got it all worked out. We haven't been seen in any house yet, and nobody can tell from our faces which is servant and which is master. So it follows: you'll be the master, Tranio, in my place, keep house, style and servants as I should. I'll be someone else: a Florentine, a Neapolitan, or some poorer man from Pisa. It's hatched, and that's how it'll be. Tranio, undress at once and take my coloured hat and cloak. When Biondello comes, he'll wait on you. But first I'll make him promise to hold his tongue.

So had you need. / In brief, sir, sith it your pleasure is, / And I am tied to be obedient; / For so your father charg'd me at our parting, / 'Be serviceable to my son,' quoth he, / Although I think 'twas in another sense: / I am content to be Lucentio, / Because so well I love Lucentio.

You'll need to. In short, sir, since that's what you want, and I'm bound to obey (because your father ordered me when we parted, "Be useful to my son," he said, though I think he meant it in another sense), I'm happy to be Lucentio, because I love Lucentio so much.
Tranio, be so, because Lucentio loves; / And let me be a slave, to achieve that maid / Whose sudden sight hath thrall'd my wounded eye.
Be him, Tranio, because Lucentio is in love. And let me be a slave, to win that girl whose sudden appearance has captured my wounded eye.
Here comes the rogue. Sirrah, where have you been?
Here comes the rascal. Where have you been, you?
Where have I been? Nay, how now! where are you? / Master, has my fellow Tranio stol'n your clothes? / Or you stol'n his? or both? Pray, what's the news?
Where have I been? No, wait, what's this? Where are you? Master, has my fellow Tranio stolen your clothes? Or have you stolen his? Or both? Please, what's going on?

Sirrah, come hither: 'tis no time to jest, / And therefore frame your manners to the time. / Your fellow Tranio here, to save my life, / Puts my apparel and my count'nance on, / And I for my escape have put on his; / For in a quarrel since I came ashore / I kill'd a man, and fear I was descried. / Wait you on him, I charge you, as becomes, / While I make way from hence to save my life. / You understand me?

Come here, you. This is no time for jokes, so behave in a way that suits the time. Your fellow Tranio here, to save my life, is putting on my clothes and my appearance, and I've put on his so I can escape. Because in a quarrel since I came ashore, I killed a man, and I'm afraid I was seen. I order you to wait on him properly while I get away from here to save my life. Do you understand me?
And not a jot of Tranio in your mouth: / Tranio is changed to Lucentio.
And not a word of Tranio from your mouth. Tranio has turned into Lucentio.
The better for him: would I were so too!
Lucky him! I wish I could too!

So could I, faith, boy, to have the next wish after, / That Lucentio indeed had Baptista's youngest daughter. / But, sirrah, not for my sake but your master's, I advise / You use your manners discreetly in all kind of companies: / When I am alone, why, then I am Tranio; / But in all places else your master, Lucentio.

So do I, believe me, boy, as long as my next wish came true: that Lucentio really did get Baptista's youngest daughter. But, you, not for my sake but for your master's, I advise you to be careful how you behave in every kind of company. When I'm alone, why then I'm Tranio. But everywhere else I'm your master, Lucentio.
Tranio, let's go. / One thing more rests, that thyself execute, / To make one among these wooers: if thou ask me why, / Sufficeth my reasons are both good and weighty.
Tranio, let's go. There's one more thing for you to do: to become one of these suitors. If you ask me why, it's enough that my reasons are good and serious.
My lord, you nod; you do not mind the play.
My lord, you're nodding off. You're not watching the play.
Yes, by Saint Anne, I do. A good matter, surely: comes there any more / of it?
Yes I am, by Saint Anne. It's good stuff, certainly. Is there any more of it?
My lord, it's only just begun.
'Tis a very excellent piece of work, madam lady: would 'twere done!
It's a really excellent piece of work, madam lady. I wish it was over!
Verona, for a while I take my leave, / To see my friends in Padua; but of all / My best beloved and approved friend, / Hortensio; and I trow this is his house. / Here, sirrah Grumio, knock, I say.
Verona, I'm leaving you for a while to see my friends in Padua, and above all my dearest and most trusted friend, Hortensio. And I think this is his house. Here, Grumio, knock, I tell you.
Knock, sir? Whom should I knock? Is there any man has rebused your / worship?
Knock, sir? Who should I knock? Has anybody insulted your worship?
Villain, I say, knock me here soundly.
You villain, I'm telling you, knock here for me, hard.
Knock you here, sir? Why, sir, what am I, sir, that I should knock you / here, sir?
Knock you here, sir? Why, sir, who am I, sir, to knock you here, sir?
Villain, I say, knock me at this gate; / And rap me well, or I'll knock your knave's pate.
Villain, I'm telling you, knock on this gate for me, and rap hard, or I'll knock your rascal's head.
My master is grown quarrelsome. I should knock you first, / And then I know after who comes by the worst.
My master has turned quarrelsome. If I knocked you first, I know who'd come off worst afterwards.
Will it not be? / Faith, sirrah, and you'll not knock, I'll ring it; / I'll try how you can sol, fa, and sing it.
Won't you do it? Well, you, if you won't knock, I'll ring it. Let's see how well you can sing your scales.
Help, masters, help! my master is mad.
Help, gentlemen, help! My master's gone mad.
Now, knock when I bid you, sirrah villain!
Now knock when I tell you, you villain!
How now! what's the matter? My old friend Grumio! and my good friend / Petruchio! How do you all at Verona?
Hello, what's the matter? My old friend Grumio! And my good friend Petruchio! How is everyone in Verona?
Signior Hortensio, come you to part the fray? / Con tutto il cuore ben trovato, may I say.
Signior Hortensio, have you come to break up the fight? With all my heart, well met, I can say.
Alla nostra casa ben venuto; molto honorato signor mio Petruchio. / Rise, Grumio, rise: we will compound this quarrel.
Welcome to our house, my most honoured Signior Petruchio. Get up, Grumio, get up. We'll settle this quarrel.

Nay, 'tis no matter, sir, what he 'leges in Latin. If this be not a / lawful cause for me to leave his service, look you, sir, he bid me / knock him and rap him soundly, sir: well, was it fit for a servant to / use his master so; being, perhaps, for aught I see, two-and-thirty, a / pip out? Whom would to God I had well knock'd at first, then had not / Grumio come by the worst.

No, it doesn't matter, sir, what he alleges in Latin. If this isn't a legal reason for me to leave his service, look here, sir: he told me to knock him and rap him hard, sir. Well, is it right for a servant to treat his master like that, when he's maybe, as far as I can see, a bit past it? I wish to God I'd knocked him hard at the start; then Grumio wouldn't have come off worst.
A senseless villain! Good Hortensio, / I bade the rascal knock upon your gate, / And could not get him for my heart to do it.
A stupid fool! Good Hortensio, I told the rascal to knock on your gate, and I couldn't for the life of me get him to do it.
Knock at the gate! O heavens! Spake you not these words plain: 'Sirrah / knock me here, rap me here, knock me well, and knock me soundly'? And / come you now with 'knocking at the gate'?
Knock at the gate! Oh heavens! Didn't you say these words plainly: "Knock me here, you, rap me here, knock me well and knock me hard"? And now you come out with "knocking at the gate"?
Sirrah, be gone, or talk not, I advise you.
Go away, you, or keep quiet, I'm warning you.

Petruchio, patience; I am Grumio's pledge; / Why, this's a heavy chance 'twixt him and you, / Your ancient, trusty, pleasant servant Grumio. / And tell me now, sweet friend, what happy gale / Blows you to Padua here from old Verona?

Patience, Petruchio. I'll vouch for Grumio. Why, this is a sad business between you and your old, trusty, amusing servant Grumio. And tell me now, dear friend, what lucky wind blows you here to Padua from old Verona?

Such wind as scatters young men through the world / To seek their fortunes farther than at home, / Where small experience grows. But in a few, / Signior Hortensio, thus it stands with me: / Antonio, my father, is deceas'd, / And I have thrust myself into this maze, / Haply to wive and thrive as best I may; / Crowns in my purse I have, and goods at home, / And so am come abroad to see the world.

The kind of wind that scatters young men around the world to seek their fortunes further away than home, where you don't learn much. But in short, Signior Hortensio, this is how things stand with me. My father, Antonio, is dead, and I've thrown myself into this maze of the world, hoping to marry and prosper as best I can. I have money in my purse and property at home, and so I've come abroad to see the world.

Petruchio, shall I then come roundly to thee / And wish thee to a shrewd ill-favour'd wife? / Thou'dst thank me but a little for my counsel; / And yet I'll promise thee she shall be rich, / And very rich: but th'art too much my friend, / And I'll not wish thee to her.

Petruchio, shall I be blunt with you and recommend you a shrewish, ugly wife? You wouldn't thank me much for the advice. And yet I promise you she'll be rich, very rich. But you're too good a friend, and I won't recommend her to you.

Signior Hortensio, 'twixt such friends as we / Few words suffice; and therefore, if thou know / One rich enough to be Petruchio's wife, / As wealth is burden of my wooing dance, / Be she as foul as was Florentius' love, / As old as Sibyl, and as curst and shrewd / As Socrates' Xanthippe or a worse, / She moves me not, or not removes, at least, / Affection's edge in me, were she as rough / As are the swelling Adriatic seas: / I come to wive it wealthily in Padua; / If wealthily, then happily in Padua.

Signior Hortensio, between friends like us, a few words are enough. So, if you know a woman rich enough to be Petruchio's wife (since wealth is the tune I dance my wooing to), she could be as ugly as the hag Florentius married, as old as the Sibyl, and as bad-tempered and shrewish as Socrates' wife Xanthippe, or worse: she won't move me, or at least she won't blunt the edge of my desire, even if she were as rough as the swelling Adriatic Sea. I've come to marry wealthily in Padua. If wealthily, then happily in Padua.

Nay, look you, sir, he tells you flatly what his mind is: why, give him / gold enough and marry him to a puppet or an aglet-baby; or an old trot / with ne'er a tooth in her head, though she have as many diseases as / two-and-fifty horses: why, nothing comes amiss, so money comes withal.

There, you see, sir, he tells you plainly what he's thinking. Why, give him enough gold and marry him to a puppet, or a tiny doll on a lace-tag, or an old hag without a tooth in her head, even if she has as many diseases as fifty-two horses. Why, nothing comes amiss, as long as money comes with it.

Petruchio, since we are stepp'd thus far in, / I will continue that I broach'd in jest. / I can, Petruchio, help thee to a wife / With wealth enough, and young and beauteous; / Brought up as best becomes a gentlewoman: / Her only fault,—and that is faults enough,— / Is, that she is intolerable curst, / And shrewd and froward, so beyond all measure, / That, were my state far worser than it is, / I would not wed her for a mine of gold.

Petruchio, since we've gone this far, I'll follow up what I started as a joke. I can help you to a wife, Petruchio, with plenty of money, young and beautiful, brought up the way a gentlewoman should be. Her only fault, and it's fault enough, is that she's unbearably bad-tempered, shrewish and difficult, so far beyond all measure that, even if I were much poorer than I am, I wouldn't marry her for a gold mine.
Hortensio, peace! thou know'st not gold's effect: / Tell me her father's name, and 'tis enough; / For I will board her, though she chide as loud / As thunder when the clouds in autumn crack.

Quiet, Hortensio! You don't know what gold can do. Tell me her father's name, and that's enough, because I'll board her like a ship, even if she scolds as loud as thunder when the autumn clouds crack.
Her father is Baptista Minola, / An affable and courteous gentleman; / Her name is Katherina Minola, / Renown'd in Padua for her scolding tongue.
Her father is Baptista Minola, a friendly and courteous gentleman. Her name is Katherina Minola, famous in Padua for her scolding tongue.

I know her father, though I know not her; / And he knew my deceased father well. / I will not sleep, Hortensio, till I see her; / And therefore let me be thus bold with you, / To give you over at this first encounter, / Unless you will accompany me thither.

I know her father, though I don't know her, and he knew my late father well. I won't sleep, Hortensio, until I've seen her. So forgive me if I'm rude enough to leave you at our very first meeting, unless you'll come there with me.

I pray you, sir, let him go while the humour lasts. O' my word, and she / knew him as well as I do, she would think scolding would do little good / upon him. She may perhaps call him half a score knaves or so; why, / that's nothing; and he begin once, he'll rail in his rope-tricks. I'll / tell you what, sir, and she stand him but a little, he will throw a / figure in her face, and so disfigure her with it that she shall have no / more eyes to see withal than a cat. You know him not, sir.

Please, sir, let him go while the mood lasts. On my word, if she knew him as well as I do, she'd realise scolding will do little good on him. She might call him a dozen rascals or so. Why, that's nothing. Once he starts, he'll rant with tricks of speech fit for the hangman's rope. I'll tell you what, sir: if she stands up to him even a little, he'll throw a figure of speech in her face and disfigure her so badly that she'll have no more eyes left to see with than a cat. You don't know him, sir.

Tarry, Petruchio, I must go with thee, / For in Baptista's keep my treasure is: / He hath the jewel of my life in hold, / His youngest daughter, beautiful Bianca, / And her withholds from me and other more, / Suitors to her and rivals in my love; / Supposing it a thing impossible, / For those defects I have before rehears'd, / That ever Katherina will be woo'd: / Therefore this order hath Baptista ta'en, / That none shall have access unto Bianca / Till Katherine the curst have got a husband.

Wait, Petruchio, I must go with you, because my treasure is in Baptista's keeping. He holds the jewel of my life, his youngest daughter, beautiful Bianca, and keeps her from me and others too, who court her and compete with me for her love. He thinks it impossible, because of the faults I've just described, that Katherina will ever be wooed. So Baptista has given this order: that nobody can visit Bianca until Katherine the shrew has got a husband.
Katherine the curst! / A title for a maid of all titles the worst.
Katherine the shrew! Of all names for a young woman, that's the worst.

Now shall my friend Petruchio do me grace, / And offer me disguis'd in sober robes, / To old Baptista as a schoolmaster / Well seen in music, to instruct Bianca; / That so I may, by this device at least / Have leave and leisure to make love to her, / And unsuspected court her by herself.

Now my friend Petruchio will do me a favour, and present me, disguised in plain clothes, to old Baptista as a schoolmaster skilled in music, to teach Bianca. That way, by this trick at least, I'll have the chance and the time to court her, and woo her alone without being suspected.
Here's no knavery! See, to beguile the old folks, how the young folks / lay their heads together!
No trickery here! Look how the young folk put their heads together to fool the old folk!
Master, master, look about you: who goes there, ha?
Master, master, look around you. Who goes there, eh?
Peace, Grumio! It is the rival of my love. Petruchio, stand by awhile.
Quiet, Grumio! It's my rival in love. Petruchio, stand aside for a while.
A proper stripling, and an amorous!
A fine young fellow, and a lover too!

O! very well; I have perus'd the note. / Hark you, sir; I'll have them very fairly bound: / All books of love, see that at any hand, / And see you read no other lectures to her. / You understand me. Over and beside / Signior Baptista's liberality, / I'll mend it with a largess. Take your papers too, / And let me have them very well perfum'd; / For she is sweeter than perfume itself / To whom they go to. What will you read to her?

Oh, very good. I've read through the list. Listen, sir, I'll have the books very handsomely bound: all books about love, make sure of that, whatever happens, and make sure you don't give her any other lessons. You understand me. On top of Signior Baptista's generosity, I'll add a tip of my own. Take your papers too, and have them well perfumed, because the lady they're going to is sweeter than perfume itself. What will you read to her?

Whate'er I read to her, I'll plead for you, / As for my patron, stand you so assur'd, / As firmly as yourself were still in place; / Yea, and perhaps with more successful words / Than you, unless you were a scholar, sir.

Whatever I read to her, I'll plead for you as my patron, you can be sure of that, as firmly as if you were there yourself. Yes, and perhaps with more successful words than yours, sir, unless you were a scholar.
O! this learning, what a thing it is.
Oh, this learning, what a thing it is!
O! this woodcock, what an ass it is.
Oh, this woodcock, what an ass he is!
Grumio, mum! God save you, Signior Gremio!
Grumio, hush! God save you, Signior Gremio!

And you are well met, Signior Hortensio. / Trow you whither I am going? To Baptista Minola. / I promis'd to enquire carefully / About a schoolmaster for the fair Bianca; / And by good fortune I have lighted well / On this young man; for learning and behaviour / Fit for her turn, well read in poetry / And other books, good ones, I warrant ye.

And good to meet you, Signior Hortensio. Do you know where I'm going? To Baptista Minola. I promised to look carefully for a schoolmaster for the fair Bianca, and by good luck I've found this young man: in learning and manners just right for her, well read in poetry and other books, good ones, I assure you.
'Tis well; and I have met a gentleman / Hath promis'd me to help me to another, / A fine musician to instruct our mistress: / So shall I no whit be behind in duty / To fair Bianca, so belov'd of me.
That's good. And I've met a gentleman who has promised to help me to another, a fine musician to teach our mistress. So I won't be one bit behind in serving fair Bianca, whom I love so much.
Belov'd of me, and that my deeds shall prove.
Whom I love, and my deeds will prove it.
[Aside] And that his bags shall prove.
And his moneybags will prove it.

Gremio, 'tis now no time to vent our love: / Listen to me, and if you speak me fair, / I'll tell you news indifferent good for either. / Here is a gentleman whom by chance I met, / Upon agreement from us to his liking, / Will undertake to woo curst Katherine; / Yea, and to marry her, if her dowry please.

Gremio, this is no time to air our love. Listen to me, and if you speak to me politely, I'll tell you news that's equally good for both of us. Here's a gentleman I met by chance who, if we agree to his terms, will undertake to woo shrewish Katherine. Yes, and marry her, if he likes the dowry.
So said, so done, is well. / Hortensio, have you told him all her faults?
No sooner said than done would be good. Hortensio, have you told him all her faults?
I know she is an irksome brawling scold; / If that be all, masters, I hear no harm.
I know she's an annoying, brawling scold. If that's all, gentlemen, I see no harm in it.
No, say'st me so, friend? What countryman?
No? You say so, friend? Where are you from?
Born in Verona, old Antonio's son. / My father dead, my fortune lives for me; / And I do hope good days and long to see.
I was born in Verona, old Antonio's son. My father's dead, my fortune lives on for me, and I hope to see good days and many of them.
O sir, such a life, with such a wife, were strange! / But if you have a stomach, to't a God's name; / You shall have me assisting you in all. / But will you woo this wild-cat?
Oh sir, such a life with such a wife would be strange! But if you have the appetite for it, go ahead in God's name. I'll help you in everything. But will you really woo this wildcat?
Will he woo her? Ay, or I'll hang her.
Will he woo her? Yes, or I'll hang her.

Why came I hither but to that intent? / Think you a little din can daunt mine ears? / Have I not in my time heard lions roar? / Have I not heard the sea, puff'd up with winds, / Rage like an angry boar chafed with sweat? / Have I not heard great ordnance in the field, / And heaven's artillery thunder in the skies? / Have I not in a pitched battle heard / Loud 'larums, neighing steeds, and trumpets' clang? / And do you tell me of a woman's tongue, / That gives not half so great a blow to hear / As will a chestnut in a farmer's fire? / Tush, tush! fear boys with bugs.

Why else did I come here but for that? Do you think a little noise can scare my ears? Haven't I in my time heard lions roar? Haven't I heard the sea, whipped up by the winds, rage like an angry boar foaming with sweat? Haven't I heard great cannon on the battlefield and heaven's artillery thundering in the sky? Haven't I heard, in a pitched battle, loud alarms, neighing horses and blaring trumpets? And you talk to me about a woman's tongue, which doesn't make half as loud a bang to the ear as a chestnut popping in a farmer's fire? Nonsense! Frighten little boys with bogeymen.
Hortensio, hark: / This gentleman is happily arriv'd, / My mind presumes, for his own good and yours.
Hortensio, listen. I think this gentleman has arrived at a lucky moment, for his own good and yours.
I promis'd we would be contributors, / And bear his charge of wooing, whatsoe'er.
I promised we would contribute and pay the costs of his wooing, whatever they are.
And so we will, provided that he win her.
And so we will, as long as he wins her.
I would I were as sure of a good dinner.
I wish I was as sure of a good dinner.
Gentlemen, God save you! If I may be bold, / Tell me, I beseech you, which is the readiest way / To the house of Signior Baptista Minola?
Gentlemen, God save you! If I may be so bold, please tell me the quickest way to the house of Signior Baptista Minola.
He that has the two fair daughters; is't he you mean?
The one with the two pretty daughters: is he the man you mean?
Hark you, sir, you mean not her to—
Listen, sir, you don't mean to court her...
Perhaps him and her, sir; what have you to do?
Perhaps him and her, sir. What business is it of yours?
Not her that chides, sir, at any hand, I pray.
Not the one who scolds, sir, at any rate, please.
I love no chiders, sir. Biondello, let's away.
I don't like scolds, sir. Biondello, let's go.
Sir, a word ere you go. / Are you a suitor to the maid you talk of, yea or no?
Sir, a word before you go. Are you a suitor to the girl you're talking about, yes or no?
And if I be, sir, is it any offence?
And if I am, sir, is that a crime?
No; if without more words you will get you hence.
No, as long as you clear off without another word.
Why, sir, I pray, are not the streets as free / For me as for you?
Why, sir, please, aren't the streets as free for me as for you?
For what reason, I beseech you?
For what reason, may I ask?
For this reason, if you'll know, / That she's the choice love of Signior Gremio.
For this reason, if you want to know: she's the chosen love of Signior Gremio.
That she's the chosen of Signior Hortensio.
She's the chosen one of Signior Hortensio.

Softly, my masters! If you be gentlemen, / Do me this right; hear me with patience. / Baptista is a noble gentleman, / To whom my father is not all unknown; / And were his daughter fairer than she is, / She may more suitors have, and me for one. / Fair Leda's daughter had a thousand wooers; / Then well one more may fair Bianca have; / And so she shall: Lucentio shall make one, / Though Paris came in hope to speed alone.

Gently, gentlemen! If you're gentlemen, do me the courtesy of hearing me out patiently. Baptista is a noble gentleman who knows something of my father. And even if his daughter were more beautiful than she is, she can have more suitors, with me as one of them. Beautiful Helen, Leda's daughter, had a thousand suitors, so fair Bianca can easily have one more. And she shall: Lucentio will be one of them, even if Paris himself came hoping to win her alone.
What, this gentleman will out-talk us all.
What! This gentleman will out-talk us all.
Sir, give him head; I know he'll prove a jade.
Sir, give him his head. I know he'll turn out to be a worn-out nag.
Hortensio, to what end are all these words?
Hortensio, what's the point of all this talk?
Sir, let me be so bold as ask you, / Did you yet ever see Baptista's daughter?
Sir, may I be so bold as to ask: have you ever actually seen Baptista's daughter?
No, sir, but hear I do that he hath two, / The one as famous for a scolding tongue / As is the other for beauteous modesty.
No, sir, but I hear he has two: one as famous for her scolding tongue as the other is for her beauty and modesty.
Sir, sir, the first's for me; let her go by.
Sir, sir, the first one's for me. Leave her alone.
Yea, leave that labour to great Hercules, / And let it be more than Alcides' twelve.
Yes, leave that job to great Hercules, and make it harder than his twelve labours.

Sir, understand you this of me, in sooth: / The youngest daughter, whom you hearken for, / Her father keeps from all access of suitors, / And will not promise her to any man / Until the elder sister first be wed; / The younger then is free, and not before.

Sir, understand this from me, honestly. The youngest daughter, the one you're after, her father keeps away from all suitors, and won't promise her to any man until the elder sister is married first. Then the younger is free, and not before.

If it be so, sir, that you are the man / Must stead us all, and me amongst the rest; / And if you break the ice, and do this feat, / Achieve the elder, set the younger free / For our access, whose hap shall be to have her / Will not so graceless be to be ingrate.

If that's so, sir, then you're the man who must help us all, me among the rest. And if you break the ice and do this deed, win the elder and free the younger for us to court, whoever is lucky enough to get her won't be so rude as to be ungrateful.
Sir, you say well, and well you do conceive; / And since you do profess to be a suitor, / You must, as we do, gratify this gentleman, / To whom we all rest generally beholding.
Sir, you speak well and think well. And since you say you're a suitor, you must reward this gentleman, as we will, since we'll all be in his debt.

Sir, I shall not be slack; in sign whereof, / Please ye we may contrive this afternoon, / And quaff carouses to our mistress' health; / And do as adversaries do in law, / Strive mightily, but eat and drink as friends.

Sir, I won't hold back. And as a sign of it, if you agree, let's spend this afternoon drinking toasts to our mistress's health, and do as opponents in a lawsuit do: fight hard, but eat and drink as friends.
O excellent motion! Fellows, let's be gone.
Oh, an excellent idea! Lads, let's go.
The motion's good indeed, and be it so:— / Petruchio, I shall be your ben venuto.
A good idea indeed, so let it be. Petruchio, I'll be your host.

Good sister, wrong me not, nor wrong yourself, / To make a bondmaid and a slave of me; / That I disdain; but for these other gawds, / Unbind my hands, I'll pull them off myself, / Yea, all my raiment, to my petticoat; / Or what you will command me will I do, / So well I know my duty to my elders.

Good sister, don't wrong me, or yourself, by making a servant and a slave of me. I hate that. But as for these other trinkets, untie my hands and I'll take them off myself, yes, all my clothes down to my petticoat. Or I'll do whatever you order me, because I know so well my duty to my elders.
Of all thy suitors here I charge thee tell / Whom thou lov'st best: see thou dissemble not.
I order you to tell me which of all your suitors here you love best. Make sure you don't lie.
Believe me, sister, of all the men alive / I never yet beheld that special face / Which I could fancy more than any other.
Believe me, sister, of all the men alive I've never yet seen that special face I could like more than any other.
Minion, thou liest. Is't not Hortensio?
You little madam, you're lying. Isn't it Hortensio?
If you affect him, sister, here I swear / I'll plead for you myself but you shall have him.
If you like him, sister, I swear here and now I'll plead for you myself, so that you'll have him.
O! then, belike, you fancy riches more: / You will have Gremio to keep you fair.
Oh, then I suppose you prefer riches. You'll have Gremio, to keep you in fine clothes.
Is it for him you do envy me so? / Nay, then you jest; and now I well perceive / You have but jested with me all this while: / I prithee, sister Kate, untie my hands.
Is it because of him that you envy me so much? No, you're joking, and now I can see you've only been joking with me all this time. Please, sister Kate, untie my hands.
If that be jest, then all the rest was so.
If that's a joke, then so was all the rest.

Why, how now, dame! Whence grows this insolence? / Bianca, stand aside. Poor girl! she weeps. / Go ply thy needle; meddle not with her. / For shame, thou hilding of a devilish spirit, / Why dost thou wrong her that did ne'er wrong thee? / When did she cross thee with a bitter word?

What's this, madam! Where does this insolence come from? Bianca, stand aside. Poor girl, she's crying. Go and do your sewing; don't have anything to do with her. For shame, you good-for-nothing with a devil's temper! Why do you hurt her, when she never hurt you? When did she ever cross you with a bitter word?
Her silence flouts me, and I'll be reveng'd.
Her silence mocks me, and I'll have my revenge.
What! in my sight? Bianca, get thee in.
What! In front of me? Bianca, go inside.

What! will you not suffer me? Nay, now I see / She is your treasure, she must have a husband; / I must dance bare-foot on her wedding-day, / And, for your love to her, lead apes in hell. / Talk not to me: I will go sit and weep / Till I can find occasion of revenge.

What! You won't put up with me? No, now I see it: she's your treasure, she must have a husband. I must dance barefoot at her wedding, like an older sister left unmarried, and because you love her I'll lead apes in hell as an old maid. Don't talk to me. I'll go and sit and cry until I can find a chance for revenge.
Was ever gentleman thus griev'd as I? / But who comes here?
Was any gentleman ever as troubled as I am? But who's this coming?
Good morrow, neighbour Gremio. God save you, gentlemen!
Good morning, neighbour Gremio. God save you, gentlemen!
And you, good sir! Pray, have you not a daughter / Call'd Katherina, fair and virtuous?
And you, good sir! Please, don't you have a daughter called Katherina, beautiful and virtuous?
I have a daughter, sir, call'd Katherina.
I have a daughter, sir, called Katherina.
You are too blunt: go to it orderly.
You're too blunt. Go about it properly.

You wrong me, Signior Gremio: give me leave. / I am a gentleman of Verona, sir, / That, hearing of her beauty and her wit, / Her affability and bashful modesty, / Her wondrous qualities and mild behaviour, / Am bold to show myself a forward guest / Within your house, to make mine eye the witness / Of that report which I so oft have heard. / And, for an entrance to my entertainment, / I do present you with a man of mine,

You're unfair to me, Signior Gremio. Let me do this. I'm a gentleman of Verona, sir, who has heard of her beauty and her wit, her friendliness and shy modesty, her wonderful qualities and mild behaviour, and so I'm bold enough to come as an eager guest to your house, to see with my own eyes the truth of what I've so often heard. And as my ticket of entry, I present you with a man of mine,
Cunning in music and the mathematics, / To instruct her fully in those sciences, / Whereof I know she is not ignorant. / Accept of him, or else you do me wrong: / His name is Licio, born in Mantua.
skilled in music and mathematics, to teach her fully in those subjects, which I know she already knows something of. Accept him, or you'll offend me. His name is Licio, born in Mantua.
Y'are welcome, sir, and he for your good sake; / But for my daughter Katherine, this I know, / She is not for your turn, the more my grief.
You're welcome, sir, and so is he, for your sake. But as for my daughter Katherine, this much I know: she isn't the right one for you, which grieves me.
I see you do not mean to part with her; / Or else you like not of my company.
I see you don't mean to part with her, or else you don't like my company.
Mistake me not; I speak but as I find. / Whence are you, sir? What may I call your name?
Don't misunderstand me. I'm only saying what I find to be true. Where are you from, sir? What's your name?
Petruchio is my name, Antonio's son; / A man well known throughout all Italy.
Petruchio is my name, Antonio's son, a man well known throughout Italy.
I know him well: you are welcome for his sake.
I knew him well. You're welcome for his sake.
Saving your tale, Petruchio, I pray, / Let us, that are poor petitioners, speak too. / Backare! you are marvellous forward.
With respect to your story, Petruchio, please let us poor petitioners speak too. Back off! You're amazingly pushy.
O, pardon me, Signior Gremio; I would fain be doing.
Oh, forgive me, Signior Gremio. I'm keen to get on with it.

I doubt it not, sir; but you will curse your wooing. Neighbour, this is / a gift very grateful, I am sure of it. To express the like kindness, / myself, that have been more kindly beholding to you than any, freely / give unto you this young scholar,

I don't doubt it, sir, but you'll curse your wooing. Neighbour, this is a very welcome gift, I'm sure. To show the same kindness myself, as I've been more kindly treated by you than anyone, I freely give you this young scholar,
that has been long studying at Rheims; as cunning in Greek, Latin, and / other languages, as the other in music and mathematics. His name is / Cambio; pray accept his service.
who has been studying for a long time at Rheims, as skilled in Greek, Latin and other languages as the other is in music and mathematics. His name is Cambio. Please accept his service.
A thousand thanks, Signior Gremio; welcome, good Cambio. [To Tranio] / But, gentle sir, methinks you walk like a stranger. May I be so bold to / know the cause of your coming?
A thousand thanks, Signior Gremio. Welcome, good Cambio. But, kind sir, you seem to be a stranger here. May I be so bold as to ask why you've come?

Pardon me, sir, the boldness is mine own, / That, being a stranger in this city here, / Do make myself a suitor to your daughter, / Unto Bianca, fair and virtuous. / Nor is your firm resolve unknown to me, / In the preferment of the eldest sister. / This liberty is all that I request, / That, upon knowledge of my parentage, / I may have welcome 'mongst the rest that woo, / And free access and favour as the rest: / And, toward the education of your daughters, / I here bestow a simple instrument, / And this small packet of Greek and Latin books: / If you accept them, then their worth is great.

Forgive me, sir, the boldness is all mine. Though I'm a stranger in this city, I'm offering myself as a suitor to your daughter, to Bianca, beautiful and virtuous. And I know your firm decision that the eldest sister must marry first. All I ask is this permission: that once you know my family, I may be welcome among the other suitors, with the same free access and favour as they have. And towards your daughters' education, I give you this simple instrument and this small parcel of Greek and Latin books. If you accept them, then they're worth a great deal.
Lucentio is your name, of whence, I pray?
Lucentio is your name? Where from, may I ask?
Of Pisa, sir; son to Vincentio.
From Pisa, sir: son of Vincentio.

A mighty man of Pisa: by report / I know him well: you are very welcome, sir. / [To Hortensio] Take you the lute, / [To Lucentio] and you the set of books; / You shall go see your pupils presently. / Holla, within!
A powerful man in Pisa. I know him well by reputation. You're very welcome, sir. You take the lute, and you the set of books. You'll go and see your pupils at once. Hello in there!
Sirrah, lead these gentlemen / To my daughters, and tell them both / These are their tutors: bid them use them well.
You, take these gentlemen to my daughters, and tell them both these are their tutors. Tell them to treat them well.
We will go walk a little in the orchard, / And then to dinner. You are passing welcome, / And so I pray you all to think yourselves.
We'll take a little walk in the orchard, and then go in to dinner. You're very welcome, and I ask you all to feel so.

Signior Baptista, my business asketh haste, / And every day I cannot come to woo. / You knew my father well, and in him me, / Left solely heir to all his lands and goods, / Which I have bettered rather than decreas'd: / Then tell me, if I get your daughter's love, / What dowry shall I have with her to wife?

Signior Baptista, my business needs speed, and I can't come wooing every day. You knew my father well, and through him you know me: the sole heir to all his lands and goods, which I've increased rather than reduced. So tell me, if I win your daughter's love, what dowry will I get with her as my wife?
After my death, the one half of my lands, / And in possession twenty thousand crowns.
After my death, half of my lands, and twenty thousand crowns in hand now.

And, for that dowry, I'll assure her of / Her widowhood, be it that she survive me, / In all my lands and leases whatsoever. / Let specialities be therefore drawn between us, / That covenants may be kept on either hand.

And in return for that dowry, I'll guarantee her, if she outlives me, a widow's share of all my lands and leases. So let's have contracts drawn up between us, so the agreements are kept on both sides.
Ay, when the special thing is well obtain'd, / That is, her love; for that is all in all.
Yes, once the special thing has been won, that is, her love, because that's all that matters.
