Why, that is nothing; for I tell you, father, / I am as peremptory as she proud-minded; / And where two raging fires meet together, / They do consume the thing that feeds their fury: / Though little fire grows great with little wind, / Yet extreme gusts will blow out fire and all; / So I to her, and so she yields to me; / For I am rough and woo not like a babe.

Why, that's nothing. I tell you, father, I'm as determined as she is proud. And when two raging fires meet, they burn up whatever feeds their fury. A little fire grows big with a little wind, but a huge gust blows out the fire and everything. That's what I'll be to her, and so she'll give in to me, because I'm rough and I don't woo like a baby.
Well mayst thou woo, and happy be thy speed! / But be thou arm'd for some unhappy words.
I hope you woo well and succeed! But be armed against some unpleasant words.
Ay, to the proof, as mountains are for winds, / That shake not though they blow perpetually.
Yes, fully armed, as mountains are against the winds, which don't shake though the winds blow for ever.
How now, my friend! Why dost thou look so pale?
What's this, my friend? Why do you look so pale?
For fear, I promise you, if I look pale.
From fear, I promise you, if I look pale.
What, will my daughter prove a good musician?
Well, will my daughter turn out to be a good musician?
I think she'll sooner prove a soldier: / Iron may hold with her, but never lutes.
I think she'll sooner turn out a soldier. Iron weapons might last with her, but never lutes.
Why, then thou canst not break her to the lute?
Why, can't you break her in to the lute, then?

Why, no; for she hath broke the lute to me. / I did but tell her she mistook her frets, / And bow'd her hand to teach her fingering; / When, with a most impatient devilish spirit, / 'Frets, call you these?' quoth she 'I'll fume with them'; / And with that word she struck me on the head, / And through the instrument my pate made way; / And there I stood amazed for a while, / As on a pillory, looking through the lute; / While she did call me rascal fiddler, / And twangling Jack, with twenty such vile terms, / As had she studied to misuse me so.

Why, no, because she's broken the lute on me. I only told her she'd got her frets wrong and bent her hand to teach her the fingering, when, with a most impatient, devilish temper, she said, "Frets, you call these? I'll fret and fume with them!" And with that she hit me on the head, and my head went through the instrument. And there I stood, dazed for a while, as if in a pillory, looking through the lute, while she called me a rascally fiddler and a twanging fool, with twenty other vile names, as if she'd practised insulting me.
Now, by the world, it is a lusty wench! / I love her ten times more than e'er I did: / O! how I long to have some chat with her!
Now, by the world, she's a lively girl! I love her ten times more than I did before. Oh, how I long to have a chat with her!

[To Hortensio] Well, go with me, and be not so discomfited; / Proceed in practice with my younger daughter; / She's apt to learn, and thankful for good turns. / Signior Petruchio, will you go with us, / Or shall I send my daughter Kate to you?

Well, come with me, and don't be so upset. Carry on teaching my younger daughter. She's quick to learn, and grateful for kindness. Signior Petruchio, will you come with us, or shall I send my daughter Kate to you?

I will attend her here, / And woo her with some spirit when she comes. / Say that she rail; why, then I'll tell her plain / She sings as sweetly as a nightingale: / Say that she frown; I'll say she looks as clear / As morning roses newly wash'd with dew: / Say she be mute, and will not speak a word; / Then I'll commend her volubility, / And say she uttereth piercing eloquence: / If she do bid me pack, I'll give her thanks, / As though she bid me stay by her a week: / If she deny to wed, I'll crave the day / When I shall ask the banns, and when be married. / But here she comes; and now, Petruchio, speak.

I'll wait for her here, and woo her with some spirit when she comes. Suppose she rants: why, then I'll tell her plainly she sings as sweetly as a nightingale. Suppose she frowns: I'll say she looks as fresh as morning roses newly washed with dew. Suppose she's silent and won't say a word: then I'll praise her talkativeness and say she speaks with stirring eloquence. If she tells me to get out, I'll thank her as if she'd asked me to stay with her a week. If she refuses to marry, I'll ask her which day I should have the banns read, and when we'll be married. But here she comes. And now, Petruchio, speak.
Good morrow, Kate; for that's your name, I hear.
Good morning, Kate, because that's your name, I hear.
Well have you heard, but something hard of hearing: / They call me Katherine that do talk of me.
You've heard well, but you're a bit hard of hearing. People who talk about me call me Katherine.

You lie, in faith, for you are call'd plain Kate, / And bonny Kate, and sometimes Kate the curst; / But, Kate, the prettiest Kate in Christendom, / Kate of Kate Hall, my super-dainty Kate, / For dainties are all Kates, and therefore, Kate, / Take this of me, Kate of my consolation; / Hearing thy mildness prais'd in every town, / Thy virtues spoke of, and thy beauty sounded,— / Yet not so deeply as to thee belongs,— / Myself am mov'd to woo thee for my wife.

You're lying, honestly, because you're called plain Kate, and pretty Kate, and sometimes Kate the shrew. But Kate, the prettiest Kate in Christendom, Kate of Kate Hall, my extra-dainty Kate (because all delicacies are "cates", and so, Kate), hear this from me, Kate of my comfort: hearing your gentleness praised in every town, your virtues talked about and your beauty proclaimed (though not as highly as you deserve), I've been moved myself to woo you as my wife.
Mov'd! in good time: let him that mov'd you hither / Remove you hence. I knew you at the first, / You were a moveable.
Moved! Well, well. Let whoever moved you here move you away again. I could tell straight away you were a piece of furniture.
Why, what's a piece of furniture?
Thou hast hit it: come, sit on me.
You've hit it. Come and sit on me.
Asses are made to bear, and so are you.
Donkeys are made to carry loads, and so are you.
Women are made to bear, and so are you.
Women are made to bear children, and so are you.
No such jade as bear you, if me you mean.
I'm not a worn-out horse that will carry you, if you mean me.
Alas! good Kate, I will not burden thee; / For, knowing thee to be but young and light,—
Oh dear, good Kate, I won't be a burden to you, because, knowing you're only young and light...
Too light for such a swain as you to catch; / And yet as heavy as my weight should be.
Too light-footed for a peasant like you to catch, and yet as heavy as I ought to be.
Ought to be! Ought to buzz!
Well ta'en, and like a buzzard.
Well caught, like a useless hawk.
O, slow-wing'd turtle! shall a buzzard take thee?
Oh, slow-winged turtle-dove! Shall a hawk catch you?
Ay, for a turtle, as he takes a buzzard.
Yes, he'll take me for a dove, as a dove takes a buzzing beetle.
Come, come, you wasp; i' faith, you are too angry.
Come, come, you wasp. Honestly, you're too angry.
If I be waspish, best beware my sting.
If I'm waspish, you'd better watch out for my sting.
My remedy is then to pluck it out.
Then my cure is to pull it out.
Ay, if the fool could find it where it lies.
Yes, if the fool could find where it is.
Who knows not where a wasp does wear his sting? / In his tail.
Who doesn't know where a wasp keeps its sting? In its tail.
Yours, if you talk of tales; and so farewell.
Yours, if you talk about tails. And so goodbye.
What! with my tongue in your tail? Nay, come again, / Good Kate; I am a gentleman.
What, with my tongue in your tail? No, come back, good Kate. I'm a gentleman.
I swear I'll cuff you if you strike again.
I swear I'll hit you if you strike me again.
So may you lose your arms: / If you strike me, you are no gentleman; / And if no gentleman, why then no arms.
Then you'll lose your coat of arms. If you hit me, you're no gentleman, and if you're no gentleman, then you have no arms.
A herald, Kate? O! put me in thy books.
An expert in heraldry, Kate? Oh, put me in your good books.
What is your crest? a coxcomb?
What's your crest? A fool's cap?
A combless cock, so Kate will be my hen.
A gentle cock without a comb, if Kate will be my hen.
No cock of mine; you crow too like a craven.
You're no cock of mine. You crow like a cowardly bird.
Nay, come, Kate, come; you must not look so sour.
No, come on, Kate, come on. You mustn't look so sour.
It is my fashion when I see a crab.
It's my habit when I see a crab apple.
Why, here's no crab, and therefore look not sour.
Why, there's no crab apple here, so don't look sour.
Had I a glass I would.
If I had a mirror I would.
Well aim'd of such a young one.
Good aim, for such a youngster.
Now, by Saint George, I am too young for you.
Now, by Saint George, I'm too young for you.
Nay, hear you, Kate: in sooth, you 'scape not so.
No, listen, Kate. Honestly, you won't get away like that.
I chafe you, if I tarry; let me go.
I'll only annoy you if I stay. Let me go.

No, not a whit; I find you passing gentle. / 'Twas told me you were rough, and coy, and sullen, / And now I find report a very liar; / For thou art pleasant, gamesome, passing courteous, / But slow in speech, yet sweet as spring-time flowers. / Thou canst not frown, thou canst not look askance, / Nor bite the lip, as angry wenches will, / Nor hast thou pleasure to be cross in talk; / But thou with mildness entertain'st thy wooers; / With gentle conference, soft and affable. / Why does the world report that Kate doth limp? / O sland'rous world! Kate like the hazel-twig / Is straight and slender, and as brown in hue / As hazel-nuts, and sweeter than the kernels. / O! let me see thee walk: thou dost not halt.

No, not a bit. I find you very gentle. I was told you were rough, standoffish and sulky, and now I find the rumours were downright lies. You're pleasant, playful, extremely polite, slow to speak, but sweet as springtime flowers. You can't frown, you can't look sideways at anyone, or bite your lip the way angry girls do, and you don't enjoy arguing. Instead you treat your suitors gently, with mild, soft and friendly talk. Why do people say Kate limps? Oh, lying world! Kate is as straight and slender as a hazel twig, as brown as hazelnuts and sweeter than their kernels. Oh, let me see you walk. You don't limp.
Go, fool, and whom thou keep'st command.
Go away, fool, and give orders to your own servants.
Did ever Dian so become a grove / As Kate this chamber with her princely gait? / O! be thou Dian, and let her be Kate, / And then let Kate be chaste, and Dian sportful!
Did Diana ever grace a forest as Kate graces this room with her royal walk? Oh, you be Diana, and let her be Kate, and then let Kate be chaste and Diana playful!
Where did you study all this goodly speech?
Where did you learn all these fine speeches?
It is extempore, from my mother-wit.
They're made up on the spot, from my natural wit.
A witty mother! witless else her son.
A witty mother! Her son would be witless without her.
Yes, clever enough to keep yourself warm.

Marry, so I mean, sweet Katherine, in thy bed; / And therefore, setting all this chat aside, / Thus in plain terms: your father hath consented / That you shall be my wife your dowry 'greed on; / And will you, nill you, I will marry you. / Now, Kate, I am a husband for your turn; / For, by this light, whereby I see thy beauty,— / Thy beauty that doth make me like thee well,— / Thou must be married to no man but me; / For I am he am born to tame you, Kate, / And bring you from a wild Kate to a Kate / Conformable as other household Kates.

Indeed, that's what I mean to do, sweet Katherine, in your bed. And so, putting all this chatter aside, here it is in plain terms. Your father has agreed that you'll be my wife. Your dowry is agreed. And whether you like it or not, I'll marry you. Now, Kate, I'm the right husband for you, because, by this daylight in which I see your beauty (the beauty that makes me like you so much), you must marry no man but me. I'm the man born to tame you, Kate, and turn you from a wild Kate into a Kate as obedient as other household cats.
Here comes your father. Never make denial; / I must and will have Katherine to my wife.
Here comes your father. Don't say no. I must and will have Katherine as my wife.
Now, Signior Petruchio, how speed you with my daughter?
Well, Signior Petruchio, how are you getting on with my daughter?
How but well, sir? how but well? / It were impossible I should speed amiss.
How else but well, sir? How else but well? It would be impossible for me to fail.
Why, how now, daughter Katherine, in your dumps?
Why, what's this, daughter Katherine? In a sulk?

Call you me daughter? Now I promise you / You have show'd a tender fatherly regard / To wish me wed to one half lunatic, / A mad-cap ruffian and a swearing Jack, / That thinks with oaths to face the matter out.

You call me daughter? Well, I promise you, you've shown great fatherly care in wanting me to marry a half-lunatic, a crazy thug and a swearing lout, who thinks he can bluff his way through with oaths.

Father, 'tis thus: yourself and all the world / That talk'd of her have talk'd amiss of her: / If she be curst, it is for policy, / For she's not froward, but modest as the dove; / She is not hot, but temperate as the morn; / For patience she will prove a second Grissel, / And Roman Lucrece for her chastity; / And to conclude, we have 'greed so well together / That upon Sunday is the wedding-day.

Father, it's like this: you and everyone who has talked about her have got her wrong. If she's shrewish, it's a tactic, because she isn't stubborn, but as gentle as a dove. She isn't hot-tempered, but as calm as the morning. In patience she'll be a second Griselda, and a Roman Lucrece in chastity. And to sum up, we've got on so well together that Sunday is the wedding day.
I'll see thee hang'd on Sunday first.
I'll see you hanged on Sunday first.
Hark, Petruchio; she says she'll see thee hang'd first.
Listen, Petruchio: she says she'll see you hanged first.
Is this your speeding? Nay, then good-night our part!
Is this your success? Well, then, goodbye to our hopes!

Be patient, gentlemen. I choose her for myself; / If she and I be pleas'd, what's that to you? / 'Tis bargain'd 'twixt us twain, being alone, / That she shall still be curst in company. / I tell you, 'tis incredible to believe / How much she loves me: O! the kindest Kate / She hung about my neck, and kiss on kiss / She vied so fast, protesting oath on oath, / That in a twink she won me to her love. / O! you are novices: 'tis a world to see, / How tame, when men and women are alone, / A meacock wretch can make the curstest shrew. / Give me thy hand, Kate; I will unto Venice, / To buy apparel 'gainst the wedding-day. / Provide the feast, father, and bid the guests; / I will be sure my Katherine shall be fine.

Be patient, gentlemen. I'm choosing her for myself. If she and I are happy, what's it to you? We agreed between the two of us, when we were alone, that she would go on being shrewish in company. I tell you, you wouldn't believe how much she loves me. Oh, the kindest Kate! She hung round my neck and piled kiss on kiss so fast, swearing vow after vow, that in a moment she won me to love her. Oh, you're beginners! It's a wonder to see how tame, when men and women are alone, a feeble coward can make the worst shrew. Give me your hand, Kate. I'll go to Venice to buy clothes for the wedding day. Get the feast ready, father, and invite the guests. I'll make sure my Katherine is finely dressed.
I know not what to say; but give me your hands. / God send you joy, Petruchio! 'Tis a match.
I don't know what to say. But give me your hands. God give you joy, Petruchio! It's a match.
Amen, say we; we will be witnesses.
Amen, we say. We'll be witnesses.
Father, and wife, and gentlemen, adieu. / I will to Venice; Sunday comes apace; / We will have rings and things, and fine array; / And kiss me, Kate; we will be married o' Sunday.
Father, and wife, and gentlemen, goodbye. I'm off to Venice. Sunday is coming fast. We'll have rings and things and fine clothes. And kiss me, Kate: we'll be married on Sunday.
Was ever match clapp'd up so suddenly?
Was a marriage ever agreed so quickly?
Faith, gentlemen, now I play a merchant's part, / And venture madly on a desperate mart.
Well, gentlemen, now I'm playing the merchant, and taking a mad gamble on a risky deal.
'Twas a commodity lay fretting by you; / 'Twill bring you gain, or perish on the seas.
It was goods that were spoiling on your hands. Now it will make you a profit, or be lost at sea.
The gain I seek is, quiet in the match.
The profit I'm looking for is peace in the marriage.
No doubt but he hath got a quiet catch. / But now, Baptista, to your younger daughter: / Now is the day we long have looked for; / I am your neighbour, and was suitor first.
No doubt he's made a peaceful catch! But now, Baptista, about your younger daughter. This is the day we've long waited for. I'm your neighbour, and I was her suitor first.
And I am one that love Bianca more / Than words can witness or your thoughts can guess.
And I'm someone who loves Bianca more than words can say or your thoughts can guess.
Youngling, thou canst not love so dear as I.
Youngster, you can't love her as dearly as I do.
But thine doth fry. / Skipper, stand back; 'tis age that nourisheth.
But yours is frying. Stand back, you young show-off. It's age that provides for a wife.
But youth in ladies' eyes that flourisheth.
But it's youth that blooms in ladies' eyes.

Content you, gentlemen; I'll compound this strife: / 'Tis deeds must win the prize, and he of both / That can assure my daughter greatest dower / Shall have my Bianca's love. / Say, Signior Gremio, what can you assure her?

Calm down, gentlemen. I'll settle this argument. It's deeds that must win the prize, and whichever of you can guarantee my daughter the bigger settlement will have my Bianca's love. Tell me, Signior Gremio, what can you guarantee her?

First, as you know, my house within the city / Is richly furnished with plate and gold: / Basins and ewers to lave her dainty hands; / My hangings all of Tyrian tapestry; / In ivory coffers I have stuff'd my crowns; / In cypress chests my arras counterpoints, / Costly apparel, tents, and canopies, / Fine linen, Turkey cushions boss'd with pearl, / Valance of Venice gold in needlework; / Pewter and brass, and all things that belong / To house or housekeeping: then, at my farm / I have a hundred milch-kine to the pail, / Six score fat oxen standing in my stalls, / And all things answerable to this portion. / Myself am struck in years, I must confess; / And if I die tomorrow this is hers, / If whilst I live she will be only mine.

First, as you know, my house in the city is richly furnished with silver and gold plate: basins and jugs to wash her dainty hands; my wall-hangings all of crimson Tyrian tapestry. I've stuffed my money into ivory boxes. In cypress-wood chests I keep my woven quilts, expensive clothes, bed-hangings and canopies, fine linen, Turkish cushions studded with pearl, Venetian bed-borders embroidered with gold thread, pewter and brass, and everything that goes with a house and housekeeping. Then at my farm I have a hundred milking cows, a hundred and twenty fat oxen in my stalls, and everything else in proportion. I'm getting on in years, I must admit, and if I die tomorrow all this is hers, as long as she'll be mine only while I'm alive.

That 'only' came well in. Sir, list to me: / I am my father's heir and only son; / If I may have your daughter to my wife, / I'll leave her houses three or four as good / Within rich Pisa's walls as anyone / Old Signior Gremio has in Padua; / Besides two thousand ducats by the year / Of fruitful land, all which shall be her jointure. / What, have I pinch'd you, Signior Gremio?

That "only" came in nicely. Sir, listen to me. I'm my father's heir and only son. If I can have your daughter as my wife, I'll leave her three or four houses inside the walls of rich Pisa, every bit as good as any old Signior Gremio has in Padua, besides two thousand ducats a year from fertile land. All of this will be her widow's settlement. What, have I pinched you, Signior Gremio?

Two thousand ducats by the year of land! / My land amounts not to so much in all: / That she shall have, besides an argosy / That now is lying in Marseilles' road. / What, have I chok'd you with an argosy?

Two thousand ducats a year from land! My land isn't worth that much altogether. Still, she'll have it all, plus a merchant ship that's now lying at anchor off Marseilles. What, have I choked you with a merchant ship?
Gremio, 'tis known my father hath no less / Than three great argosies, besides two galliasses, / And twelve tight galleys; these I will assure her, / And twice as much, whate'er thou offer'st next.

Gremio, everyone knows my father has no fewer than three great merchant ships, besides two big galleys and twelve sturdy smaller ones. I'll guarantee her these, and twice as much as whatever you offer next.
Nay, I have offer'd all; I have no more; / And she can have no more than all I have; / If you like me, she shall have me and mine.
No, I've offered everything. I've nothing more. And she can't have more than everything I have. If you like me, she'll have me and all that's mine.
Why, then the maid is mine from all the world, / By your firm promise; Gremio is out-vied.
Why, then the girl is mine above everyone in the world, by your firm promise. Gremio is outbid.
I must confess your offer is the best; / And let your father make her the assurance, / She is your own; else, you must pardon me; / If you should die before him, where's her dower?
I must admit your offer is the best. And if your father guarantees it to her, she's yours. Otherwise, you must forgive me: if you died before him, where would her settlement be?
That's but a cavil; he is old, I young.
That's just a quibble. He's old, and I'm young.
And may not young men die as well as old?
And can't young men die as well as old ones?

Well, gentlemen, / I am thus resolv'd. On Sunday next, you know, / My daughter Katherine is to be married; / Now, on the Sunday following, shall Bianca / Be bride to you, if you make this assurance; / If not, to Signior Gremio. / And so I take my leave, and thank you both.

Well, gentlemen, this is what I've decided. Next Sunday, as you know, my daughter Katherine is to be married. Now, on the following Sunday, Bianca will be your bride, if you make this guarantee. If not, she'll be Signior Gremio's. And so I'll say goodbye, and thank you both.
Now, I fear thee not: / Sirrah young gamester, your father were a fool / To give thee all, and in his waning age / Set foot under thy table. Tut! a toy! / An old Italian fox is not so kind, my boy.

Now I'm not afraid of you. You young gambler, your father would be a fool to give you everything and then, in his old age, live off your charity. Nonsense! A joke! An old Italian fox isn't so generous, my boy.

A vengeance on your crafty wither'd hide! / Yet I have fac'd it with a card of ten. / 'Tis in my head to do my master good: / I see no reason but suppos'd Lucentio / Must get a father, call'd suppos'd Vincentio; / And that's a wonder: fathers commonly / Do get their children; but in this case of wooing / A child shall get a sire, if I fail not of my cunning.

Curse your sly, wrinkled skin! Still, I've bluffed it out with a ten. I've got an idea to help my master. I see no other way: the supposed Lucentio must produce a father, called the supposed Vincentio. And that's a wonder: usually fathers produce their children, but in this case of wooing, a child will produce a father, if my cunning doesn't fail me.
Fiddler, forbear; you grow too forward, sir. / Have you so soon forgot the entertainment / Her sister Katherine welcome'd you withal?
Fiddler, stop it. You're getting too pushy, sir. Have you forgotten so soon the welcome her sister Katherine gave you?
But, wrangling pedant, this is / The patroness of heavenly harmony: / Then give me leave to have prerogative; / And when in music we have spent an hour, / Your lecture shall have leisure for as much.
But, you quarrelsome schoolteacher, this lady is the patron of heavenly harmony. So let me go first, and when we've spent an hour on music, your lesson can have the same amount of time.

Preposterous ass, that never read so far / To know the cause why music was ordain'd! / Was it not to refresh the mind of man / After his studies or his usual pain? / Then give me leave to read philosophy, / And while I pause serve in your harmony.

You absurd ass, you never read enough to know why music was created! Wasn't it to refresh the human mind after study or ordinary work? So let me teach philosophy, and when I stop, you can serve up your harmony.
Sirrah, I will not bear these braves of thine.
You, I won't put up with your insults.

Why, gentlemen, you do me double wrong, / To strive for that which resteth in my choice. / I am no breeching scholar in the schools, / I'll not be tied to hours nor 'pointed times, / But learn my lessons as I please myself. / And, to cut off all strife, here sit we down; / Take you your instrument, play you the whiles; / His lecture will be done ere you have tun'd.

Why, gentlemen, you do me a double wrong in fighting over something that's for me to choose. I'm not a schoolboy who can be whipped. I won't be tied to timetables and set hours; I'll learn my lessons as I please. And to end all this argument, let's sit down here. You take your instrument and play meanwhile. His lesson will be over before you've tuned up.
You'll leave his lecture when I am in tune?
You'll stop his lesson when I'm in tune?
That will be never: tune your instrument.
That will be never. Tune your instrument.
Where did we stop last time?
Here, madam:— / Hic ibat Simois; hic est Sigeia tellus; / Hic steterat Priami regia celsa senis.
Here, madam: "Here flowed the river Simois; here is the land of Sigeia; here stood the lofty palace of old Priam."

Hic ibat, as I told you before, Simois, I am Lucentio, hic est, / son unto Vincentio of Pisa, Sigeia tellus, disguised thus to get your / love, Hic steterat, and that Lucentio that comes a-wooing, Priami, / is my man Tranio, regia, bearing my port, celsa senis, that we / might beguile the old pantaloon.

"Hic ibat", as I told you before, "Simois", I am Lucentio, "hic est", son of Vincentio of Pisa, "Sigeia tellus", disguised like this to win your love, "Hic steterat", and that Lucentio who comes wooing, "Priami", is my servant Tranio, "regia", playing my part, "celsa senis", so that we could fool the old dotard.
Oh dear! The top string is out of tune.
Spit in the hole, man, and tune again.
Spit in the peg-hole, man, and tune it again.

Now let me see if I can construe it: Hic ibat Simois, I know you not; / hic est Sigeia tellus, I trust you not; Hic steterat Priami, take / heed he hear us not; regia, presume not; celsa senis, despair not.

Now let me see if I can translate it. "Hic ibat Simois", I don't know you; "hic est Sigeia tellus", I don't trust you; "Hic steterat Priami", be careful he doesn't hear us; "regia", don't presume; "celsa senis", don't despair.
The base is right; 'tis the base knave that jars. / [Aside] How fiery and forward our pedant is! / Now, for my life, the knave doth court my love: / Pedascule, I'll watch you better yet.

The bass is right. It's the base rascal that's out of tune. How fiery and pushy our schoolteacher is! Now, on my life, the scoundrel is courting my love. Little pedant, I'll watch you more closely yet.
In time I may believe, yet I mistrust.
In time I may believe it, but for now I don't trust it.
Mistrust it not; for sure, Æacides / Was Ajax, call'd so from his grandfather.
Don't doubt it, because Aeacides was certainly Ajax, named after his grandfather.

I must believe my master; else, I promise you, / I should be arguing still upon that doubt; / But let it rest. Now, Licio, to you. / Good master, take it not unkindly, pray, / That I have been thus pleasant with you both.

I must believe my teacher. Otherwise, I promise you, I'd still be arguing about that question. But let it be. Now, Licio, your turn. Good teachers, please don't be offended that I've been so playful with you both.
[To Lucentio] You may go walk and give me leave a while; / My lessons make no music in three parts.
You can go for a walk and leave me alone for a while. My lessons aren't music for three voices.
Are you so formal, sir? Well, I must wait, / [Aside] And watch withal; for, but I be deceiv'd, / Our fine musician groweth amorous.
Are you so particular, sir? Well, I must wait, and keep watch too, because unless I'm mistaken, our fine musician is falling in love.

Madam, before you touch the instrument, / To learn the order of my fingering, / I must begin with rudiments of art; / To teach you gamut in a briefer sort, / More pleasant, pithy, and effectual, / Than hath been taught by any of my trade: / And there it is in writing, fairly drawn.

Madam, before you touch the instrument and learn how I place my fingers, I must start with the basics of the art, to teach you the scale in a shorter way, more pleasant, concise and effective than anyone in my trade has taught it. And there it is, written out neatly.
Why, I am past my gamut long ago.
Why, I left the scale behind long ago.
Yet read the gamut of Hortensio.

[Reads] Gamut I am, the ground of all accord, / A re, to plead Hortensio's passion; / B mi, Bianca, take him for thy lord, / C fa ut, that loves with all affection: / D sol re, one clef, two notes have I / E la mi, show pity or I die. / Call you this gamut? Tut, I like it not: / Old fashions please me best; I am not so nice, / To change true rules for odd inventions.

"Gamut, I am the foundation of all harmony. A re: to plead Hortensio's passion. B mi: Bianca, take him for your husband. C fa ut: who loves you with all his heart. D sol re: one clef, two notes I have. E la mi: show pity or I'll die." You call this a scale? Nonsense, I don't like it. The old ways please me best. I'm not so silly as to swap true rules for strange new inventions.
Mistress, your father prays you leave your books, / And help to dress your sister's chamber up: / You know tomorrow is the wedding-day.
Mistress, your father asks you to leave your books and help to decorate your sister's room. You know tomorrow is the wedding day.
Farewell, sweet masters, both: I must be gone.
Goodbye, dear teachers, both of you. I must go.
Faith, mistress, then I have no cause to stay.
Well, mistress, then I have no reason to stay.

But I have cause to pry into this pedant: / Methinks he looks as though he were in love. / Yet if thy thoughts, Bianca, be so humble / To cast thy wand'ring eyes on every stale, / Seize thee that list: if once I find thee ranging, / Hortensio will be quit with thee by changing.

But I have reason to look into this schoolteacher. I think he looks as if he's in love. Still, Bianca, if your thoughts are so low that you cast your wandering eyes on any decoy, let whoever wants you have you. If I ever find you straying, Hortensio will get even with you by changing to someone else.

[To Tranio] / Signior Lucentio, this is the 'pointed day / That Katherine and Petruchio should be married, / And yet we hear not of our son-in-law. / What will be said? What mockery will it be / To want the bridegroom when the priest attends / To speak the ceremonial rites of marriage! / What says Lucentio to this shame of ours?

Signior Lucentio, this is the day appointed for Katherine and Petruchio's wedding, and yet we've heard nothing from our son-in-law. What will people say? What a mockery it will be to have no bridegroom when the priest is ready to perform the marriage ceremony! What does Lucentio say to this shame of ours?

No shame but mine; I must, forsooth, be forc'd / To give my hand, oppos'd against my heart, / Unto a mad-brain rudesby, full of spleen; / Who woo'd in haste and means to wed at leisure. / I told you, I, he was a frantic fool, / Hiding his bitter jests in blunt behaviour; / And to be noted for a merry man, / He'll woo a thousand, 'point the day of marriage, / Make friends, invite, and proclaim the banns; / Yet never means to wed where he hath woo'd. / Now must the world point at poor Katherine, / And say 'Lo! there is mad Petruchio's wife, / If it would please him come and marry her.'

The shame is mine alone. I must, indeed, be forced to give my hand against my heart's wishes to a mad, rude, hot-tempered man who wooed in a hurry and means to marry at his leisure. I told you, I did, that he was a raving fool, hiding his bitter jokes behind rough manners. And to be known as a merry fellow, he'll woo a thousand women, set the wedding day, make friends, invite guests and announce the banns, and yet never mean to marry the woman he's wooed. Now the world will point at poor Katherine and say, "Look, there's mad Petruchio's wife, if he'd only come and marry her."

Patience, good Katherine, and Baptista too. / Upon my life, Petruchio means but well, / Whatever fortune stays him from his word: / Though he be blunt, I know him passing wise; / Though he be merry, yet withal he's honest.

Patience, good Katherine, and Baptista too. On my life, Petruchio means well, whatever accident is keeping him from his word. Though he's blunt, I know he's very wise; though he's merry, he's honest too.
Would Katherine had never seen him though!
I wish Katherine had never seen him!
Go, girl, I cannot blame thee now to weep, / For such an injury would vex a very saint; / Much more a shrew of thy impatient humour.
Go, girl. I can't blame you for crying now, because such an insult would annoy a saint, let alone a shrew with your impatient temper.
Master, master! News! old news, and such news as you never heard of!
Master, master! News! Old news, and news like you've never heard!
Is it new and old too? How may that be?
New and old at once? How can that be?
Why, is it not news to hear of Petruchio's coming?
Why, isn't it news to hear that Petruchio is coming?
When he stands where I am and sees you there.
When he's standing where I am and sees you there.
But say, what to thine old news?
But tell us, what about your old news?

Why, Petruchio is coming, in a new hat and an old jerkin; a pair of old / breeches thrice turned; a pair of boots that have been candle-cases, / one buckled, another laced; an old rusty sword ta'en out of the town / armoury, with a broken hilt, and chapeless; with two broken points: his / horse hipped with an old mothy saddle and stirrups of no kindred; / besides, possessed with the glanders and like to mose in the chine; / troubled with the lampass, infected with the fashions, full of / windgalls, sped with spavins, rayed with the yellows, past cure of the / fives, stark spoiled with the staggers, begnawn with the bots, swayed / in the back and shoulder-shotten; near-legged before, and with a / half-checked bit, and a head-stall of sheep's leather, which, being / restrained to keep him from stumbling, hath been often burst, and now / repaired with knots; one girth six times pieced, and a woman's crupper / of velure, which hath two letters for her name fairly set down in / studs, and here and there pieced with pack-thread.

Why, Petruchio is coming in a new hat and an old jacket; a pair of old breeches turned inside out three times; a pair of boots that have been used to keep candle-ends in, one buckled, the other laced; an old rusty sword taken from the town armoury, with a broken handle and no tip to its sheath, and two broken laces. His horse is lame in the hip, with an old moth-eaten saddle and stirrups that don't match. What's more, it has glanders and is likely to have a rotting spine; it's troubled with swollen gums, infected with farcy, full of swollen leg joints, ruined by spavin, discoloured with jaundice, past any cure for the vives, completely wrecked by staggers, gnawed by worms, sway-backed, with a dislocated shoulder and knock-kneed in front. It has a half-checked bit and a head-strap of sheep's leather which, having been pulled tight to stop the horse stumbling, has often broken and is now mended with knots; one belly-strap has been patched six times, and it has a woman's velvet crupper, with her two initials neatly set out in studs, and patched here and there with string.

O, sir! his lackey, for all the world caparisoned like the horse; with / a linen stock on one leg and a kersey boot-hose on the other, gartered / with a red and blue list; an old hat, and the humour of forty fancies / prick'd in't for a feather: a monster, a very monster in apparel, and / not like a Christian footboy or a gentleman's lackey.

Oh, sir, his servant, decked out exactly like the horse: a linen stocking on one leg and a coarse woollen sock on the other, tied with red and blue strips of cloth; an old hat with some crazy decoration stuck in it for a feather. A monster, a real monster in his clothes, not like any Christian page or a gentleman's servant.
'Tis some odd humour pricks him to this fashion; / Yet oftentimes he goes but mean-apparell'd.
It's some strange whim that drives him to dress like this. Still, he often goes about in plain clothes.
I am glad he's come, howsoe'er he comes.
I'm glad he's come, however he comes.
Didst thou not say he comes?
No, sir; I say his horse comes, with him on his back.
No, sir. I said his horse is coming, with him on its back.
Nay, by Saint Jamy, / I hold you a penny, / A horse and a man / Is more than one, / And yet not many.
No, by Saint James, I'll bet you a penny, a horse and a man are more than one, and yet not many.
Come, where be these gallants? Who is at home?
Come on, where are these fine gentlemen? Who's at home?
And yet I come not well.
And yet I don't come well.
Not so well apparell'd as I wish you were.
Not as well dressed as I'd like you to be.

Were it better, I should rush in thus. / But where is Kate? Where is my lovely bride? / How does my father? Gentles, methinks you frown; / And wherefore gaze this goodly company, / As if they saw some wondrous monument, / Some comet or unusual prodigy?

Even if I were better dressed, I'd rush in like this. But where's Kate? Where's my lovely bride? How is my father? Gentlemen, you seem to be frowning. And why is this fine company staring as if they'd seen some amazing omen, some comet or strange portent?

Why, sir, you know this is your wedding-day: / First were we sad, fearing you would not come; / Now sadder, that you come so unprovided. / Fie! doff this habit, shame to your estate, / An eye-sore to our solemn festival.

Why, sir, you know this is your wedding day. First we were sad, afraid you wouldn't come; now we're sadder that you've come so badly prepared. Shame on you! Take off these clothes. They're a disgrace to your position and an eyesore at our solemn celebration.
And tell us what occasion of import / Hath all so long detain'd you from your wife, / And sent you hither so unlike yourself?
And tell us what important business has kept you so long from your wife, and sent you here so unlike yourself.

Tedious it were to tell, and harsh to hear; / Sufficeth I am come to keep my word, / Though in some part enforced to digress; / Which at more leisure I will so excuse / As you shall well be satisfied withal. / But where is Kate? I stay too long from her; / The morning wears, 'tis time we were at church.

It would be tedious to tell and unpleasant to hear. It's enough that I've come to keep my word, though I was forced to turn aside for a while. I'll explain it later in a way that will satisfy you. But where's Kate? I've been away from her too long. The morning's passing; it's time we were at church.
See not your bride in these unreverent robes; / Go to my chamber, put on clothes of mine.
Don't see your bride in these disrespectful clothes. Go to my room and put on some of mine.
Not I, believe me: thus I'll visit her.
Not me, believe me. I'll visit her like this.
But thus, I trust, you will not marry her.
But you won't marry her like this, I hope.

Good sooth, even thus; therefore ha' done with words; / To me she's married, not unto my clothes. / Could I repair what she will wear in me / As I can change these poor accoutrements, / 'Twere well for Kate and better for myself. / But what a fool am I to chat with you / When I should bid good morrow to my bride, / And seal the title with a lovely kiss!

Indeed I will, just like this. So stop talking. She's marrying me, not my clothes. If I could repair what she'll wear out in me as easily as I can change these poor outfits, it would be good for Kate and better for me. But what a fool I am to chat with you when I should be saying good morning to my bride and sealing my claim with a lovely kiss!
He hath some meaning in his mad attire. / We will persuade him, be it possible, / To put on better ere he go to church.
There's some meaning behind his mad clothes. We'll persuade him, if we can, to put on something better before he goes to church.
I'll after him and see the event of this.
I'll follow him and see how this turns out.

But, sir, to love concerneth us to add / Her father's liking; which to bring to pass, / As I before imparted to your worship, / I am to get a man,—whate'er he be / It skills not much; we'll fit him to our turn,— / And he shall be Vincentio of Pisa, / And make assurance here in Padua, / Of greater sums than I have promised. / So shall you quietly enjoy your hope, / And marry sweet Bianca with consent.

But, sir, to her love we need to add her father's approval. To bring that about, as I told your worship before, I'm going to find a man (it doesn't matter much who he is; we'll train him for our purpose), and he'll pretend to be Vincentio of Pisa and guarantee here in Padua even bigger sums than I've promised. That way you'll calmly get what you hope for and marry sweet Bianca with her father's consent.

Were it not that my fellow schoolmaster / Doth watch Bianca's steps so narrowly, / 'Twere good, methinks, to steal our marriage; / Which once perform'd, let all the world say no, / I'll keep mine own despite of all the world.

If it weren't that my fellow schoolteacher watches Bianca's every step so closely, I think it would be a good idea to marry her in secret. Once it's done, let the whole world say no, I'll keep what's mine in spite of the whole world.

That by degrees we mean to look into, / And watch our vantage in this business. / We'll over-reach the greybeard, Gremio, / The narrow-prying father, Minola, / The quaint musician, amorous Licio; / All for my master's sake, Lucentio.

We'll look into that step by step and watch for our chance in this business. We'll outwit the greybeard Gremio, the nosy father Minola and the crafty musician, lovesick Licio, all for my master Lucentio's sake.
Signior Gremio, came you from the church?
Signior Gremio, have you come from the church?
As willingly as e'er I came from school.
As gladly as I ever came out of school.
And is the bride and bridegroom coming home?
And are the bride and bridegroom coming home?
A bridegroom, say you? 'Tis a groom indeed, / A grumbling groom, and that the girl shall find.
A bridegroom, you say? He's a stable-groom, more like, a grumbling groom, and the girl will find that out.
Worse-tempered than her? Why, that's impossible.
Why, he's a devil, a devil, a very fiend.
Why, he's a devil, a devil, a real fiend.
Why, she's a devil, a devil, the devil's dam.
Why, she's a devil, a devil, the devil's mother.

Tut! she's a lamb, a dove, a fool, to him. / I'll tell you, Sir Lucentio: when the priest / Should ask if Katherine should be his wife, / 'Ay, by gogs-wouns' quoth he, and swore so loud / That, all amaz'd, the priest let fall the book; / And as he stoop'd again to take it up, / The mad-brain'd bridegroom took him such a cuff / That down fell priest and book, and book and priest: / 'Now take them up,' quoth he 'if any list.'

Nonsense! She's a lamb, a dove, a fool compared with him. I'll tell you, Signior Lucentio: when the priest asked whether Katherine should be his wife, "Yes, by God's wounds!" he said, and swore so loud that the priest, astonished, dropped the book. And as he bent down to pick it up, the mad bridegroom gave him such a cuff that down fell priest and book, book and priest. "Now pick them up," he said, "if anyone wants to."
What said the wench, when he rose again?
What did the girl say when he got up again?

Trembled and shook, for why, he stamp'd and swore / As if the vicar meant to cozen him. / But after many ceremonies done, / He calls for wine: 'A health!' quoth he, as if / He had been abroad, carousing to his mates / After a storm; quaff'd off the muscadel, / And threw the sops all in the sexton's face, / Having no other reason / But that his beard grew thin and hungerly / And seem'd to ask him sops as he was drinking. / This done, he took the bride about the neck, / And kiss'd her lips with such a clamorous smack / That at the parting all the church did echo. / And I, seeing this, came thence for very shame; / And after me, I know, the rout is coming. / Such a mad marriage never was before. / Hark, hark! I hear the minstrels play.

She trembled and shook, because he stamped and swore as if the vicar meant to cheat him. But after all the ceremonies were done, he called for wine. "A toast!" he said, as if he'd been on board ship drinking with his shipmates after a storm. He gulped down the sweet wine and threw the bread soaked in it right in the sexton's face, for no other reason than that the sexton's beard grew thin and hungry-looking and seemed to be begging him for the bread while he was drinking. That done, he took the bride round the neck and kissed her lips with such a loud smack that the whole church echoed as they parted. And when I saw this, I left out of sheer embarrassment. And after me, I know, the crowd is coming. There's never been such a mad wedding. Listen, listen! I can hear the musicians playing.

Gentlemen and friends, I thank you for your pains: / I know you think to dine with me today, / And have prepar'd great store of wedding cheer / But so it is, my haste doth call me hence, / And therefore here I mean to take my leave.

Gentlemen and friends, thank you for your trouble. I know you expect to dine with me today, and have prepared plenty of wedding food. But the fact is, my urgent business calls me away, and so I mean to say goodbye here.
Is't possible you will away tonight?
Is it possible you'll leave tonight?

I must away today before night come. / Make it no wonder: if you knew my business, / You would entreat me rather go than stay. / And, honest company, I thank you all, / That have beheld me give away myself / To this most patient, sweet, and virtuous wife. / Dine with my father, drink a health to me. / For I must hence; and farewell to you all.

I must leave today, before night comes. Don't be surprised. If you knew my business, you'd beg me to go rather than stay. And, good company, thank you all for watching me give myself away to this most patient, sweet and virtuous wife. Dine with my father-in-law and drink a toast to me, because I must go. And goodbye to you all.
Let us entreat you stay till after dinner.
Let us beg you to stay until after dinner.
I am content you shall entreat me stay; / But yet not stay, entreat me how you can.
I'm content for you to beg me to stay. But I won't stay, however you beg me.
Now, if you love me, stay.
Now, if you love me, stay.
Ay, sir, they be ready; the oats have eaten the horses.
Yes, sir, they're ready. The oats have eaten the horses.

Nay, then, / Do what thou canst, I will not go today; / No, nor tomorrow, not till I please myself. / The door is open, sir; there lies your way; / You may be jogging whiles your boots are green; / For me, I'll not be gone till I please myself. / 'Tis like you'll prove a jolly surly groom / That take it on you at the first so roundly.

Well, then, do what you like, I won't go today. No, nor tomorrow, not until I please. The door's open, sir; there's your way out. You can be trotting off while your boots are still fresh. As for me, I won't go until I please. You'll likely turn out a fine, surly husband, since you take charge so bluntly from the start.
O Kate! content thee: prithee be not angry.
Oh, Kate! Calm down. Please don't be angry.
I will be angry: what hast thou to do? / Father, be quiet; he shall stay my leisure.
I will be angry. What business is it of yours? Father, keep quiet. He'll stay until I'm ready.
Ay, marry, sir, now it begins to work.
Yes, indeed, sir, now it's starting to work.
Gentlemen, forward to the bridal dinner: / I see a woman may be made a fool, / If she had not a spirit to resist.
Gentlemen, go on in to the wedding dinner. I see a woman can be made a fool of, if she hasn't the spirit to resist.

They shall go forward, Kate, at thy command. / Obey the bride, you that attend on her; / Go to the feast, revel and domineer, / Carouse full measure to her maidenhead, / Be mad and merry, or go hang yourselves: / But for my bonny Kate, she must with me. / Nay, look not big, nor stamp, nor stare, nor fret; / I will be master of what is mine own. / She is my goods, my chattels; she is my house, / My household stuff, my field, my barn, / My horse, my ox, my ass, my anything; / And here she stands, touch her whoever dare; / I'll bring mine action on the proudest he / That stops my way in Padua. Grumio, / Draw forth thy weapon; we are beset with thieves; / Rescue thy mistress, if thou be a man. / Fear not, sweet wench; they shall not touch thee, Kate; / I'll buckler thee against a million.

They shall go forward, Kate, at your command. Obey the bride, all you who serve her. Go to the feast, celebrate and live it up, drink deep toasts to her virginity, be mad and merry, or go and hang yourselves. But as for my pretty Kate, she must come with me. No, don't look angry, or stamp, or stare, or fret. I'll be master of what's my own. She's my goods, my possessions. She's my house, my household furniture, my field, my barn, my horse, my ox, my donkey, my anything. And here she stands: let anyone touch her who dares. I'll take the law on the proudest man who blocks my way in Padua. Grumio, draw your weapon. We're surrounded by thieves. Rescue your mistress, if you're a man. Don't be afraid, sweet girl. They won't touch you, Kate. I'll shield you against a million.
Nay, let them go, a couple of quiet ones.
No, let them go, a quiet pair.
Went they not quickly, I should die with laughing.
If they hadn't gone so quickly, I'd have died laughing.
Of all mad matches, never was the like.
Of all mad marriages, there's never been one like it.
Mistress, what's your opinion of your sister?
Mistress, what do you think of your sister?
That, being mad herself, she's madly mated.
That, being mad herself, she's madly matched.
I warrant him, Petruchio is Kated.
I'll bet Petruchio has been Kated.

Neighbours and friends, though bride and bridegroom wants / For to supply the places at the table, / You know there wants no junkets at the feast. / Lucentio, you shall supply the bridegroom's place; / And let Bianca take her sister's room.

Neighbours and friends, though the bride and groom aren't here to fill their places at the table, you know there's no shortage of sweets at the feast. Lucentio, you take the bridegroom's place, and let Bianca take her sister's.
Shall sweet Bianca practise how to bride it?
Shall sweet Bianca practise being a bride?
She shall, Lucentio. Come, gentlemen, let's go.
She shall, Lucentio. Come, gentlemen, let's go.

Fie, fie on all tired jades, on all mad masters, and all foul ways! Was / ever man so beaten? Was ever man so ray'd? Was ever man so weary? I am / sent before to make a fire, and they are coming after to warm them. / Now, were not I a little pot and soon hot, my very lips might freeze to / my teeth, my tongue to the roof of my mouth, my heart in my belly, ere / I should come by a fire to thaw me. But I with blowing the fire shall / warm myself; for, considering the weather, a taller man than I will / take cold. Holla, ho! Curtis!

Curse all worn-out nags, all mad masters and all filthy roads! Was any man ever so beaten? Was any man ever so covered in mud? Was any man ever so tired? I'm sent ahead to make a fire, and they're coming after to warm themselves. Now, if I weren't a little pot that heats up quickly, my lips might freeze to my teeth, my tongue to the roof of my mouth and my heart to my belly before I could get to a fire to thaw me. But I'll warm myself by blowing on the fire, because in this weather a taller man than me would catch cold. Hello there! Curtis!
Who is that calls so coldly?
A piece of ice: if thou doubt it, thou mayst slide from my shoulder to / my heel with no greater a run but my head and my neck. A fire, good / Curtis.
A lump of ice. If you doubt it, you can slide from my shoulder to my heel with no bigger run-up than my head and neck. A fire, good Curtis.
Is my master and his wife coming, Grumio?
Are my master and his wife coming, Grumio?
O, ay! Curtis, ay; and therefore fire, fire; cast on no water.
Oh yes, Curtis, yes. And so, fire, fire. Don't throw any water on it.
Is she so hot a shrew as she's reported?
Is she as hot-tempered a shrew as people say?
She was, good Curtis, before this frost; but thou knowest winter tames / man, woman, and beast; for it hath tamed my old master, and my new / mistress, and myself, fellow Curtis.
She was, good Curtis, before this frost. But you know winter tames man, woman and beast. It has tamed my old master, my new mistress and myself, friend Curtis.
Away, you three-inch fool! I am no beast.
Get away, you three-inch fool! I'm no beast.

Am I but three inches? Why, thy horn is a foot; and so long am I at the / least. But wilt thou make a fire, or shall I complain on thee to our / mistress, whose hand,—she being now at hand,— thou shalt soon feel, to / thy cold comfort, for being slow in thy hot office?

Am I only three inches? Why, your cuckold's horn is a foot long, and I'm at least that long. But will you make a fire, or shall I complain about you to our mistress? You'll soon feel her hand, now she's close at hand, and it'll be cold comfort to you for being slow at your hot job.
I prithee, good Grumio, tell me, how goes the world?
Please, good Grumio, tell me, how are things?
A cold world, Curtis, in every office but thine; and therefore fire. Do / thy duty, and have thy duty, for my master and mistress are almost / frozen to death.
It's a cold world, Curtis, in every job except yours, so: fire. Do your duty and get your due, because my master and mistress are almost frozen to death.
There's fire ready; and therefore, good Grumio, the news.
The fire's ready. So, good Grumio, the news.
Why, 'Jack boy! ho, boy!' and as much news as wilt thou.
Why, "Jack, boy! Ho, boy!", as in the song, and as much news as you like.
Come, you are so full of cony-catching.
Come on, you're so full of tricks.

Why, therefore, fire; for I have caught extreme cold. Where's the cook? / Is supper ready, the house trimmed, rushes strewed, cobwebs swept, the / servingmen in their new fustian, their white stockings, and every / officer his wedding-garment on? Be the Jacks fair within, the Jills / fair without, and carpets laid, and everything in order?

Why, then, fire, because I've caught a terrible cold. Where's the cook? Is supper ready, the house tidied, fresh rushes laid on the floor, cobwebs swept, the servants in their new work clothes and white stockings, and every officer of the house in his wedding outfit? Are the jacks clean inside and the jills clean outside, the tablecloths laid and everything in order?
All ready; and therefore, I pray thee, news.
All ready. So, please, the news.
First, know my horse is tired; my master and mistress fallen out.
First, you should know my horse is tired, and my master and mistress have fallen out.
Out of their saddles into the dirt; and thereby hangs a tale.
Out of their saddles into the mud. And that's the start of a story.
This 'tis to feel a tale, not to hear a tale.
This is feeling a story, not hearing one.
And therefore 'tis called a sensible tale; and this cuff was but to / knock at your ear and beseech listening. Now I begin: Imprimis, we / came down a foul hill, my master riding behind my mistress,—
And so it's called a story you can feel. And that cuff was only to knock on your ear and ask it to listen. Now I'll begin. Firstly, we came down a muddy hill, my master riding behind my mistress...

Tell thou the tale: but hadst thou not crossed me, thou shouldst have / heard how her horse fell, and she under her horse; thou shouldst have / heard in how miry a place, how she was bemoiled; how he left her with / the horse upon her; how he beat me because her horse stumbled; how she / waded through the dirt to pluck him off me: how he swore; how she / prayed, that never prayed before; how I cried; how the horses ran away; / how her bridle was burst; how I lost my crupper; with many things of / worthy memory, which now shall die in oblivion, and thou return / unexperienced to thy grave.

You tell the story, then. But if you hadn't interrupted me, you'd have heard how her horse fell, and she was under her horse; you'd have heard what a muddy place it was, how she got covered in mud, how he left her with the horse on top of her, how he beat me because her horse stumbled, how she waded through the mud to pull him off me, how he swore, how she prayed, who never prayed before, how I cried, how the horses ran away, how her bridle broke, how I lost my crupper, and many other things worth remembering, which will now die forgotten, and you'll go to your grave without knowing them.
By this reckoning he is more shrew than she.
By this account, he's more of a shrew than she is.

Ay; and that thou and the proudest of you all shall find when he comes / home. But what talk I of this? Call forth Nathaniel, Joseph, Nicholas, / Philip, Walter, Sugarsop, and the rest; let their heads be sleekly / combed, their blue coats brush'd and their garters of an indifferent / knit; let them curtsy with their left legs, and not presume to touch a / hair of my master's horse-tail till they kiss their hands. Are they all / ready?

Yes, and you and the proudest of you will find that out when he gets home. But why am I talking about this? Call out Nathaniel, Joseph, Nicholas, Philip, Walter, Sugarsop and the rest. Make sure their hair is combed smooth, their blue coats brushed and their garters matching. Have them bow with their left legs and not dare to touch a hair of my master's horse's tail until they've kissed their hands. Are they all ready?
Do you hear? ho! You must meet my master to countenance my mistress.
Do you hear? Hey! You must go and meet my master to give my mistress a proper welcome.
Why, she hath a face of her own.
Why, she has a face of her own.
Thou, it seems, that calls for company to countenance her.
You, it seems, if you're calling for people to give her a face.
I call them forth to credit her.
I'm calling them out to do her credit.
Why, she comes to borrow nothing of them.
Why, she isn't coming to borrow anything from them.
Welcome, you; how now, you; what, you; fellow, you; and thus much for / greeting. Now, my spruce companions, is all ready, and all things neat?
Welcome, you; hello, you; well, you; friend, you. And that's enough greetings. Now, my smart friends, is everything ready and everything neat?
All things is ready. How near is our master?
Everything's ready. How close is our master?
E'en at hand, alighted by this; and therefore be not,— / Cock's passion, silence! I hear my master.
Almost here; he's dismounted by now. And so don't be... By God's passion, quiet! I can hear my master.
Where be these knaves? What! no man at door / To hold my stirrup nor to take my horse? / Where is Nathaniel, Gregory, Philip?—
Where are these rascals? What, no man at the door to hold my stirrup or take my horse? Where are Nathaniel, Gregory, Philip?
Here, sir! here, sir! here, sir! here, sir! / You logger-headed and unpolish'd grooms! / What, no attendance? no regard? no duty? / Where is the foolish knave I sent before?
Here, sir! Here, sir! Here, sir! Here, sir! You blockheaded, uncouth stable-boys! What, no service? No respect? No duty? Where's the foolish rascal I sent ahead?
Here, sir; as foolish as I was before.
Here, sir, as foolish as I was before.
You peasant swain! you whoreson malt-horse drudge! / Did I not bid thee meet me in the park, / And bring along these rascal knaves with thee?
You peasant clod! You bastard, you cart-horse drudge! Didn't I tell you to meet me in the park and bring these rascals with you?

Nathaniel's coat, sir, was not fully made, / And Gabriel's pumps were all unpink'd i' the heel; / There was no link to colour Peter's hat, / And Walter's dagger was not come from sheathing; / There was none fine but Adam, Ralph, and Gregory; / The rest were ragged, old, and beggarly; / Yet, as they are, here are they come to meet you.

Nathaniel's coat, sir, wasn't finished, and Gabriel's shoes weren't decorated at the heel. There was no soot to blacken Peter's hat, and Walter's dagger hadn't come back from having its sheath made. None of them were smart except Adam, Ralph and Gregory. The rest were ragged, old and shabby. Still, such as they are, here they are to meet you.
Go, rascals, go and fetch my supper in.
Go, you rascals, go and bring my supper in.
Where is the life that late I led? / Where are those—? / Sit down, Kate, and welcome. / Food, food, food, food!
"Where is the life that I led lately? Where are those...?" Sit down, Kate, and welcome. Food, food, food, food!

Why, when, I say?—Nay, good sweet Kate, be merry.— / Off with my boots, you rogues! you villains! when? / It was the friar of orders grey, / As he forth walked on his way: / Out, you rogue! you pluck my foot awry:

Why, when will it come, I say? No, good sweet Kate, be cheerful. Get my boots off, you rogues! You villains! When? "It was the grey-robed friar, as he walked along his way." Get out, you rogue! You're twisting my foot.
Take that, and mend the plucking off the other. / Be merry, Kate. Some water, here; what, ho! / Where's my spaniel Troilus? Sirrah, get you hence / And bid my cousin Ferdinand come hither:
Take that, and do a better job pulling off the other one. Be cheerful, Kate. Some water here! Hey there! Where's my spaniel Troilus? You, get out of here and tell my cousin Ferdinand to come here.
One, Kate, that you must kiss and be acquainted with. / Where are my slippers? Shall I have some water? / Come, Kate, and wash, and welcome heartily.—
One you must kiss and get to know, Kate. Where are my slippers? Will I get some water? Come, Kate, wash your hands, and a hearty welcome to you.
You whoreson villain! will you let it fall?
You bastard villain! Will you drop it?
Patience, I pray you; 'twas a fault unwilling.
Patience, please. It was an accident.
A whoreson, beetle-headed, flap-ear'd knave! / Come, Kate, sit down; I know you have a stomach. / Will you give thanks, sweet Kate, or else shall I?— / What's this? Mutton?
A bastard, blockheaded, floppy-eared rascal! Come, Kate, sit down. I know you're hungry. Will you say grace, sweet Kate, or shall I? What's this? Mutton?
'Tis burnt; and so is all the meat. / What dogs are these! Where is the rascal cook? / How durst you, villains, bring it from the dresser, / And serve it thus to me that love it not?
It's burnt, and so is all the meat. What dogs these are! Where's that rascal of a cook? How dare you villains bring it from the kitchen and serve it like this to me, when I don't like it?
There, take it to you, trenchers, cups, and all. / You heedless joltheads and unmanner'd slaves! / What! do you grumble? I'll be with you straight.
There, take it all back, plates, cups and everything. You thoughtless blockheads and ill-mannered slaves! What, are you muttering? I'll deal with you in a moment.
I pray you, husband, be not so disquiet; / The meat was well, if you were so contented.
Please, husband, don't be so upset. The meat was fine, if you'd been happy with it.

I tell thee, Kate, 'twas burnt and dried away, / And I expressly am forbid to touch it; / For it engenders choler, planteth anger; / And better 'twere that both of us did fast, / Since, of ourselves, ourselves are choleric, / Than feed it with such over-roasted flesh. / Be patient; tomorrow 't shall be mended. / And for this night we'll fast for company: / Come, I will bring thee to thy bridal chamber.

I tell you, Kate, it was burnt and dried up, and I'm strictly forbidden to touch it, because it produces bile and breeds anger. And it would be better for both of us to go hungry, since we're both naturally hot-tempered, than to feed that temper with overcooked meat. Be patient. Tomorrow it will be put right, and for tonight we'll both go without, to keep each other company. Come, I'll take you to your bridal chamber.
Peter, didst ever see the like?
Peter, did you ever see anything like it?
He kills her in her own humour.
He's beating her at her own game.

In her chamber, making a sermon of continency to her; / And rails, and swears, and rates, that she, poor soul, / Knows not which way to stand, to look, to speak, / And sits as one new risen from a dream. / Away, away! for he is coming hither.

In her room, preaching her a sermon on self-control. And he rants and swears and scolds, so that she, poor soul, doesn't know which way to stand, to look, or to speak, and sits like someone just woken from a dream. Away, away! He's coming this way.

Thus have I politicly begun my reign, / And 'tis my hope to end successfully. / My falcon now is sharp and passing empty. / And till she stoop she must not be full-gorg'd, / For then she never looks upon her lure. / Another way I have to man my haggard, / To make her come, and know her keeper's call, / That is, to watch her, as we watch these kites / That bate and beat, and will not be obedient. / She eat no meat today, nor none shall eat; / Last night she slept not, nor tonight she shall not; / As with the meat, some undeserved fault / I'll find about the making of the bed; / And here I'll fling the pillow, there the bolster, / This way the coverlet, another way the sheets; / Ay, and amid this hurly I intend / That all is done in reverend care of her; / And, in conclusion, she shall watch all night: / And if she chance to nod I'll rail and brawl, / And with the clamour keep her still awake. / This is a way to kill a wife with kindness; / And thus I'll curb her mad and headstrong humour. / He that knows better how to tame a shrew, / Now let him speak; 'tis charity to show.

So I've begun my reign with cunning, and I hope to end it successfully. My falcon is now keen and very hungry, and until she comes down to the lure she mustn't be fully fed, because then she never looks at the lure. I have another way to tame my wild hawk, to make her come and know her keeper's call: that is, to keep her awake, as we do with those hawks that flap and struggle and won't obey. She ate no food today, and she won't eat any. Last night she didn't sleep, and tonight she won't either. As with the meat, I'll find some made-up fault in the way the bed is made, and I'll throw the pillow here, the bolster there, the bedspread this way and the sheets that way. Yes, and in all this commotion I'll pretend it's all done out of loving care for her. In the end, she'll stay awake all night. And if she happens to nod off, I'll rant and shout and keep her awake with the noise. This is the way to kill a wife with kindness, and so I'll curb her mad and headstrong temper. If anyone knows a better way to tame a shrew, let him speak now. It would be a kindness to share it.
Is 't possible, friend Licio, that Mistress Bianca / Doth fancy any other but Lucentio? / I tell you, sir, she bears me fair in hand.
Is it possible, friend Licio, that Mistress Bianca loves anyone but Lucentio? I tell you, sir, she's encouraging me.
Sir, to satisfy you in what I have said, / Stand by and mark the manner of his teaching.
Sir, to prove what I've said, stand aside and watch how he teaches.
Now, mistress, profit you in what you read?
Now, mistress, are you getting anything out of what you're reading?
What, master, read you? First resolve me that.
What are you reading, master? Answer me that first.
I read that I profess, The Art to Love.
I'm reading what I practise: The Art of Love.
And may you prove, sir, master of your art!
And may you prove a master of your art, sir!
While you, sweet dear, prove mistress of my heart.
While you, sweet darling, prove the mistress of my heart.
Quick proceeders, marry! Now tell me, I pray, / You that durst swear that your Mistress Bianca / Lov'd none in the world so well as Lucentio.
Quick learners, indeed! Now tell me, please, you who dared to swear that your Mistress Bianca loved nobody in the world as much as Lucentio.
O despiteful love! unconstant womankind! / I tell thee, Licio, this is wonderful.
Oh, spiteful love! Fickle women! I tell you, Licio, this is astonishing.

Mistake no more; I am not Licio. / Nor a musician as I seem to be; / But one that scorn to live in this disguise / For such a one as leaves a gentleman / And makes a god of such a cullion: / Know, sir, that I am call'd Hortensio.

Don't be mistaken any longer. I'm not Licio, or a musician as I seem to be, but someone who refuses to go on in this disguise for a woman who leaves a gentleman and makes a god of a low rascal like that. Know, sir, that my name is Hortensio.

Signior Hortensio, I have often heard / Of your entire affection to Bianca; / And since mine eyes are witness of her lightness, / I will with you, if you be so contented, / Forswear Bianca and her love for ever.
Signior Hortensio, I've often heard of your complete devotion to Bianca. And since my own eyes have seen her flightiness, I'll join you, if you agree, in renouncing Bianca and her love for ever.

See, how they kiss and court! Signior Lucentio, / Here is my hand, and here I firmly vow / Never to woo her more, but do forswear her, / As one unworthy all the former favours / That I have fondly flatter'd her withal.

Look how they kiss and court! Signior Lucentio, here's my hand, and here I firmly swear never to woo her again, but to renounce her, as unworthy of all the favours I foolishly flattered her with before.
And here I take the like unfeigned oath, / Never to marry with her though she would entreat; / Fie on her! See how beastly she doth court him!
And here I take the same sincere oath: never to marry her, even if she begged me. Shame on her! Look how shamelessly she courts him!

Would all the world but he had quite forsworn! / For me, that I may surely keep mine oath, / I will be married to a wealthy widow / Ere three days pass, which hath as long lov'd me / As I have lov'd this proud disdainful haggard. / And so farewell, Signior Lucentio. / Kindness in women, not their beauteous looks, / Shall win my love; and so I take my leave, / In resolution as I swore before.

I wish everyone in the world except him had given her up! As for me, to make sure I keep my oath, I'll marry a rich widow before three days are out, who has loved me as long as I've loved this proud, scornful wild hawk. And so goodbye, Signior Lucentio. Kindness in women, not their beautiful looks, will win my love. And so I'll say goodbye, as determined as I swore before.
Mistress Bianca, bless you with such grace / As 'longeth to a lover's blessed case! / Nay, I have ta'en you napping, gentle love, / And have forsworn you with Hortensio.
Mistress Bianca, may you be blessed with all the grace that belongs to a lover's happy state! Yes, I've caught you napping, sweet love, and have renounced you along with Hortensio.
Tranio, you jest; but have you both forsworn me?
You're joking, Tranio. But have you both really renounced me?
Then we are rid of Licio.
I' faith, he'll have a lusty widow now, / That shall be woo'd and wedded in a day.
Honestly, he'll have a lively widow now, who'll be wooed and married in a day.
Faith, he is gone unto the taming-school.
Honestly, he's gone to the taming school.
The taming-school! What, is there such a place?
The taming school! What, is there such a place?
Ay, mistress; and Petruchio is the master, / That teacheth tricks eleven and twenty long, / To tame a shrew and charm her chattering tongue.
Yes, mistress, and Petruchio is the headmaster. He teaches every trick in the book to tame a shrew and silence her chattering tongue.
O master, master! I have watch'd so long / That I am dog-weary; but at last I spied / An ancient angel coming down the hill / Will serve the turn.
Oh master, master! I've been watching so long that I'm dog-tired, but at last I've spotted an old fellow coming down the hill who'll do the job.
Master, a mercatante or a pedant, / I know not what; but formal in apparel, / In gait and countenance surely like a father.
Master, a merchant or a schoolmaster, I don't know which, but he's formally dressed, and in his walk and his face he certainly looks like a father.
If he be credulous and trust my tale, / I'll make him glad to seem Vincentio, / And give assurance to Baptista Minola, / As if he were the right Vincentio. / Take in your love, and then let me alone.

If he's gullible and believes my story, I'll make him glad to pretend to be Vincentio and give guarantees to Baptista Minola as if he were the real Vincentio. Take your love inside, and then leave it to me.
And you, sir! you are welcome. / Travel you far on, or are you at the farthest?
And you, sir! You're welcome. Are you travelling far, or have you reached the end of your journey?
Sir, at the farthest for a week or two; / But then up farther, and as far as Rome; / And so to Tripoli, if God lend me life.
Sir, this is as far as I go for a week or two, but then I go further, as far as Rome, and on to Tripoli, if God lets me live.
Where are you from, may I ask?
Of Mantua, sir? Marry, God forbid, / And come to Padua, careless of your life!
From Mantua, sir? God forbid! And you've come to Padua, so careless of your life!
My life, sir! How, I pray? for that goes hard.
My life, sir! How, please? That sounds serious.

'Tis death for anyone in Mantua / To come to Padua. Know you not the cause? / Your ships are stay'd at Venice; and the Duke,— / For private quarrel 'twixt your Duke and him,— / Hath publish'd and proclaim'd it openly. / 'Tis marvel, but that you are but newly come / You might have heard it else proclaim'd about.

It's death for anyone from Mantua to come to Padua. Don't you know why? Your ships are being held at Venice, and the Duke, because of a private quarrel between your Duke and him, has publicly announced it. It's a wonder, though since you've only just arrived, you might not have heard it proclaimed around.
Alas, sir! it is worse for me than so; / For I have bills for money by exchange / From Florence, and must here deliver them.
Oh dear, sir! It's worse for me than that, because I'm carrying bills of exchange from Florence that I must cash here.
Well, sir, to do you courtesy, / This will I do, and this I will advise you: / First, tell me, have you ever been at Pisa?
Well, sir, to do you a kindness, this is what I'll do, and this is my advice. First, tell me, have you ever been to Pisa?
Ay, sir, in Pisa have I often been, / Pisa renowned for grave citizens.
Yes, sir, I've often been to Pisa, Pisa famous for its serious citizens.
Among them know you one Vincentio?
Do you know a man called Vincentio among them?
I know him not, but I have heard of him, / A merchant of incomparable wealth.
I don't know him, but I've heard of him: a merchant of unequalled wealth.
He is my father, sir; and, sooth to say, / In countenance somewhat doth resemble you.
He's my father, sir. And to tell the truth, he looks a little like you.
[Aside] As much as an apple doth an oyster, and all one.
As much as an apple looks like an oyster, it's all the same.

To save your life in this extremity, / This favour will I do you for his sake; / And think it not the worst of all your fortunes / That you are like to Sir Vincentio. / His name and credit shall you undertake, / And in my house you shall be friendly lodg'd; / Look that you take upon you as you should! / You understand me, sir; so shall you stay / Till you have done your business in the city. / If this be courtesy, sir, accept of it.

To save your life in this emergency, I'll do you this favour for his sake, and you'll count it not the worst of your luck that you look like Signior Vincentio. You'll take on his name and reputation, and you'll be put up as a friend in my house. Make sure you play the part properly! You understand me, sir. You'll stay like that until you've done your business in the city. If this is a kindness, sir, accept it.
O, sir, I do; and will repute you ever / The patron of my life and liberty.
Oh, sir, I do, and I'll always think of you as the saviour of my life and freedom.

Then go with me to make the matter good. / This, by the way, I let you understand: / My father is here look'd for every day / To pass assurance of a dower in marriage / 'Twixt me and one Baptista's daughter here: / In all these circumstances I'll instruct you. / Go with me to clothe you as becomes you.

Then come with me and we'll put it into action. And by the way, I should tell you: my father is expected here any day, to guarantee a marriage settlement between me and the daughter of a man called Baptista here. I'll teach you all the details. Come with me and we'll dress you as you should be.
No, no, forsooth; I dare not for my life.
No, no, really. I wouldn't dare, for my life.

The more my wrong, the more his spite appears. / What, did he marry me to famish me? / Beggars that come unto my father's door / Upon entreaty have a present alms; / If not, elsewhere they meet with charity; / But I, who never knew how to entreat, / Nor never needed that I should entreat, / Am starv'd for meat, giddy for lack of sleep; / With oaths kept waking, and with brawling fed. / And that which spites me more than all these wants, / He does it under name of perfect love; / As who should say, if I should sleep or eat / 'Twere deadly sickness, or else present death. / I prithee go and get me some repast; / I care not what, so it be wholesome food.

The more I'm wronged, the more his spite shows. What, did he marry me to starve me? Beggars who come to my father's door get charity straight away when they ask for it; if not, they find charity somewhere else. But I, who never knew how to beg and never needed to, am starved of food, dizzy from lack of sleep, kept awake by swearing and fed on shouting. And what annoys me more than all I'm going without, he does it in the name of perfect love, as if to say that if I slept or ate it would make me deathly ill, or kill me at once. Please go and get me something to eat. I don't care what, as long as it's wholesome food.
What say you to a neat's foot?
What do you say to a calf's foot?
'Tis passing good; I prithee let me have it.
That's very good. Please let me have it.
I fear it is too choleric a meat. / How say you to a fat tripe finely broil'd?
I'm afraid it's too bile-making a food. What do you say to a fat tripe, nicely grilled?
I like it well; good Grumio, fetch it me.
I'd like that. Good Grumio, fetch it for me.
