I cannot tell; I fear 'tis choleric. / What say you to a piece of beef and mustard?
I don't know. I'm afraid it's bile-making. What do you say to a piece of beef and mustard?
A dish that I do love to feed upon.
A dish I love to eat.
Ay, but the mustard is too hot a little.
Yes, but the mustard is a little too hot.
Why then the beef, and let the mustard rest.
Why then, the beef, and forget the mustard.
Nay, then I will not: you shall have the mustard, / Or else you get no beef of Grumio.
No, then I won't. You'll have the mustard, or you'll get no beef from Grumio.
Then both, or one, or anything thou wilt.
Then both, or one, or anything you like.
Why then the mustard without the beef.
Why then, the mustard without the beef.
Go, get thee gone, thou false deluding slave,
Go on, get out, you lying, cheating slave,
That feed'st me with the very name of meat. / Sorrow on thee and all the pack of you / That triumph thus upon my misery! / Go, get thee gone, I say.
who feeds me on nothing but the names of food! Curse you and the whole pack of you who gloat like this over my misery! Go, get out, I tell you.
How fares my Kate? What, sweeting, all amort?
How is my Kate? What, sweetheart, so downcast?
Faith, as cold as can be.
Honestly, as cold as can be.
Pluck up thy spirits; look cheerfully upon me. / Here, love; thou seest how diligent I am, / To dress thy meat myself, and bring it thee:
Cheer up. Look at me cheerfully. Here, love: you see how attentive I am, cooking your food myself and bringing it to you.
I am sure, sweet Kate, this kindness merits thanks. / What! not a word? Nay, then thou lov'st it not, / And all my pains is sorted to no proof. / Here, take away this dish.
I'm sure, sweet Kate, this kindness deserves thanks. What, not a word? No, then you don't like it, and all my trouble has come to nothing. Here, take this dish away.
I pray you, let it stand.
The poorest service is repaid with thanks; / And so shall mine, before you touch the meat.
The smallest service is repaid with thanks, and so shall mine be, before you touch the food.
Signior Petruchio, fie! you are to blame. / Come, Mistress Kate, I'll bear you company.
Signior Petruchio, shame on you! You're in the wrong. Come, Mistress Kate, I'll keep you company.

[Aside] Eat it up all, Hortensio, if thou lovest me. / Much good do it unto thy gentle heart! / Kate, eat apace: and now, my honey love, / Will we return unto thy father's house / And revel it as bravely as the best, / With silken coats and caps, and golden rings, / With ruffs and cuffs and farthingales and things; / With scarfs and fans and double change of bravery, / With amber bracelets, beads, and all this knavery. / What! hast thou din'd? The tailor stays thy leisure, / To deck thy body with his ruffling treasure.

Eat it all up, Hortensio, if you love me. Much good may it do your kind heart! Kate, eat quickly. And now, my honey love, we'll go back to your father's house and celebrate as splendidly as anyone, with silk coats and caps and golden rings, with ruffs and cuffs and hooped petticoats and things, with scarves and fans and two changes of fine clothes, with amber bracelets, beads and all this frippery. What, have you finished eating? The tailor is waiting for you, to dress your body in his frilly treasures.
Come, tailor, let us see these ornaments; / Lay forth the gown.—
Come, tailor, let's see these decorations. Lay out the gown.
Here is the cap your worship did bespeak.
Here's the cap your worship ordered.

Why, this was moulded on a porringer; / A velvet dish: fie, fie! 'tis lewd and filthy: / Why, 'tis a cockle or a walnut-shell, / A knack, a toy, a trick, a baby's cap: / Away with it! come, let me have a bigger.

Why, this was shaped on a soup bowl: a velvet dish. Ugh, ugh! It's vulgar and nasty. Why, it's a cockleshell or a walnut shell, a knick-knack, a toy, a trinket, a baby's cap. Take it away! Come on, give me a bigger one.
I'll have no bigger; this doth fit the time, / And gentlewomen wear such caps as these.
I won't have a bigger one. This one is in fashion, and gentlewomen wear caps like these.
When you are gentle, you shall have one too, / And not till then.
When you're gentle, you'll have one too, and not till then.
[Aside] That will not be in haste.
That won't be any time soon.

Why, sir, I trust I may have leave to speak; / And speak I will. I am no child, no babe. / Your betters have endur'd me say my mind, / And if you cannot, best you stop your ears. / My tongue will tell the anger of my heart, / Or else my heart, concealing it, will break; / And rather than it shall, I will be free / Even to the uttermost, as I please, in words.

Why, sir, I trust I'm allowed to speak, and speak I will. I'm no child, no baby. Better men than you have put up with me speaking my mind, and if you can't, you'd better block your ears. My tongue will express the anger in my heart, or else my heart will break from hiding it. And rather than let that happen, I'll be free to say exactly what I please, to the very limit.
Why, thou say'st true; it is a paltry cap, / A custard-coffin, a bauble, a silken pie; / I love thee well in that thou lik'st it not.
Why, you're right. It's a paltry cap, a pie crust, a trinket, a silk pie. I love you all the more for not liking it.
Love me or love me not, I like the cap; / And it I will have, or I will have none.
Love me or don't love me, I like the cap, and I'll have it or none at all.

Thy gown? Why, ay: come, tailor, let us see't. / O mercy, God! what masquing stuff is here? / What's this? A sleeve? 'Tis like a demi-cannon. / What, up and down, carv'd like an apple tart? / Here's snip and nip and cut and slish and slash, / Like to a censer in a barber's shop. / Why, what i' devil's name, tailor, call'st thou this?

Your gown? Why, yes. Come, tailor, let's see it. Oh God have mercy! What fancy-dress costume is this? What's this? A sleeve? It's like a cannon. What, carved up and down like an apple tart? Here's snipping and nipping and cutting and slitting and slashing, like an incense burner in a barber's shop. Why, what in the devil's name, tailor, do you call this?
[Aside] I see she's like to have neither cap nor gown.
I can see she's likely to get neither cap nor gown.
You bid me make it orderly and well, / According to the fashion and the time.
You told me to make it properly and well, in the latest fashion.

Marry, and did; but if you be remember'd, / I did not bid you mar it to the time. / Go, hop me over every kennel home, / For you shall hop without my custom, sir. / I'll none of it: hence! make your best of it.

Indeed I did. But if you remember, I didn't tell you to ruin it for the sake of fashion. Go on, hop home over every gutter, because you'll be hopping without my business, sir. I'll have none of it. Get out! Do what you like with it.
I never saw a better fashion'd gown, / More quaint, more pleasing, nor more commendable; / Belike you mean to make a puppet of me.
I never saw a better-made gown, more elegant, more pleasing or more praiseworthy. I suppose you mean to make a puppet of me.
Why, true; he means to make a puppet of thee.
Why, that's right: he means to make a puppet of you.
She says your worship means to make a puppet of her.
She says your worship means to make a puppet of her.

O monstrous arrogance! Thou liest, thou thread, / Thou thimble, / Thou yard, three-quarters, half-yard, quarter, nail! / Thou flea, thou nit, thou winter-cricket thou! / Brav'd in mine own house with a skein of thread! / Away! thou rag, thou quantity, thou remnant, / Or I shall so be-mete thee with thy yard / As thou shalt think on prating whilst thou liv'st! / I tell thee, I, that thou hast marr'd her gown.

Oh, outrageous arrogance! You liar, you thread, you thimble, you yard, three-quarters, half-yard, quarter, inch! You flea, you nit, you winter cricket! Insulted in my own house by a reel of thread! Get out, you rag, you scrap, you leftover, or I'll measure you with your own yardstick so that you'll think twice about chattering for the rest of your life! I tell you, I do, you've ruined her gown.
Your worship is deceiv'd: the gown is made / Just as my master had direction. / Grumio gave order how it should be done.
Your worship is mistaken. The gown is made exactly as my master was instructed. Grumio gave orders how it should be made.
I gave him no order; I gave him the stuff.
I gave him no orders. I gave him the material.
But how did you desire it should be made?
But how did you want it made?
Marry, sir, with needle and thread.
Why, sir, with needle and thread.
But did you not request to have it cut?
But didn't you ask to have it cut?

Face not me. Thou hast braved many men; brave not me: I will neither be / fac'd nor brav'd. I say unto thee, I bid thy master cut out the gown; / but I did not bid him cut it to pieces: ergo, thou liest.

Don't try to face me down. You've dressed up plenty of men; don't try to dress me down. I won't be faced or braved. I tell you, I told your master to cut out the gown, but I didn't tell him to cut it to pieces. Therefore, you're lying.
Why, here is the note of the fashion to testify.
Why, here's the written order to prove it.
The note lies in 's throat, if he say I said so.
The order is a downright liar if it says I said that.
Master, if ever I said loose-bodied gown, sew me in the skirts of it / and beat me to death with a bottom of brown thread; I said, a gown.
Master, if I ever said a loose gown, sew me up in its skirts and beat me to death with a reel of brown thread. I said a gown.
Error i' the bill, sir; error i' the bill. I commanded the sleeves / should be cut out, and sew'd up again; and that I'll prove upon thee, / though thy little finger be armed in a thimble.
A mistake in the order, sir, a mistake in the order. I ordered the sleeves to be cut out and sewn up again, and I'll prove it on you in a fight, even if your little finger is armed with a thimble.
This is true that I say; and I had thee in place where thou shouldst / know it.
What I say is true. And if I had you in the right place, you'd know it.
I am for thee straight; take thou the bill, give me thy mete-yard, and / spare not me.
I'm ready for you now. You take the order, give me your yardstick, and don't hold back.
God-a-mercy, Grumio! Then he shall have no odds.
God have mercy, Grumio! Then he'll have no chance.
Well, sir, in brief, the gown is not for me.
Well, sir, in short, the gown is not for me.
You are i' the right, sir; 'tis for my mistress.
You're right, sir. It's for my mistress.
Go, take it up unto thy master's use.
Go, take it away for your master to use.
Villain, not for thy life! Take up my mistress' gown for thy master's / use!
Villain, not for your life! Lift up my mistress's gown for your master to use!
Why, sir, what's your conceit in that?
Why, sir, what do you mean by that?
O, sir, the conceit is deeper than you think for. / Take up my mistress' gown to his master's use! / O fie, fie, fie!
Oh, sir, the meaning is deeper than you think. Lift up my mistress's gown for his master's use! Oh, shame, shame, shame!
[Aside] Hortensio, say thou wilt see the tailor paid. / [To Tailor] Go take it hence; be gone, and say no more.
Hortensio, say you'll see the tailor gets paid. Go, take it away. Clear off and say no more.
[Aside to Tailor] Tailor, I'll pay thee for thy gown tomorrow; / Take no unkindness of his hasty words. / Away, I say! commend me to thy master.
Tailor, I'll pay you for your gown tomorrow. Don't be offended by his hasty words. Go, I tell you. Give my regards to your master.

Well, come, my Kate; we will unto your father's / Even in these honest mean habiliments. / Our purses shall be proud, our garments poor / For 'tis the mind that makes the body rich; / And as the sun breaks through the darkest clouds, / So honour peereth in the meanest habit. / What, is the jay more precious than the lark / Because his feathers are more beautiful? / Or is the adder better than the eel / Because his painted skin contents the eye? / O no, good Kate; neither art thou the worse / For this poor furniture and mean array. / If thou account'st it shame, lay it on me; / And therefore frolic; we will hence forthwith, / To feast and sport us at thy father's house. / Go call my men, and let us straight to him; / And bring our horses unto Long-lane end; / There will we mount, and thither walk on foot. / Let's see; I think 'tis now some seven o'clock, / And well we may come there by dinner-time.

Well, come on, my Kate. We'll go to your father's in these honest, plain clothes. Our purses will be proud and our clothes poor, because it's the mind that makes the body rich. And as the sun breaks through the darkest clouds, so honour shines through the plainest clothes. What, is the jay more precious than the lark because its feathers are more beautiful? Or is the adder better than the eel because its patterned skin pleases the eye? Oh no, good Kate. You aren't any the worse for these poor clothes and plain outfit. If you think it shameful, blame me. So cheer up. We'll leave at once to feast and enjoy ourselves at your father's house. Go and call my men, and let's go to him straight away. Bring our horses to the end of Long Lane. We'll mount there, and walk on foot till then. Let's see. I think it's about seven o'clock now, and we can easily get there by lunchtime.
I dare assure you, sir, 'tis almost two, / And 'twill be supper-time ere you come there.
I assure you, sir, it's almost two, and it'll be suppertime before you get there.

It shall be seven ere I go to horse. / Look what I speak, or do, or think to do, / You are still crossing it. Sirs, let 't alone: / I will not go today; and ere I do, / It shall be what o'clock I say it is.

It will be seven before I get on my horse. Look, whatever I say, or do, or think of doing, you're always contradicting it. Gentlemen, forget it. I won't go today, and before I do, it'll be whatever time I say it is.
Why, so this gallant will command the sun.
Why, at this rate this fine fellow will give orders to the sun.
Sir, this is the house; please it you that I call?
Sir, this is the house. Shall I call?
Ay, what else? and, but I be deceived, / Signior Baptista may remember me, / Near twenty years ago in Genoa, / Where we were lodgers at the Pegasus.
Yes, what else? And unless I'm mistaken, Signior Baptista may remember me from nearly twenty years ago in Genoa, when we were both staying at the Pegasus inn.
'Tis well; and hold your own, in any case, / With such austerity as 'longeth to a father.
Good. And in any case, play your part with the seriousness that suits a father.
I warrant you. But, sir, here comes your boy; / 'Twere good he were school'd.
I promise you. But, sir, here comes your servant. It would be good to coach him.
Fear you not him. Sirrah Biondello, / Now do your duty throughly, I advise you. / Imagine 'twere the right Vincentio.
Don't worry about him. Biondello, now do your job thoroughly, I advise you. Imagine this is the real Vincentio.
But hast thou done thy errand to Baptista?
But have you done your errand to Baptista?
I told him that your father was at Venice, / And that you look'd for him this day in Padua.
I told him your father was in Venice, and that you expected him in Padua today.
Th'art a tall fellow; hold thee that to drink. / Here comes Baptista. Set your countenance, sir.
You're a fine fellow. Take that and buy yourself a drink. Here comes Baptista. Put on the right expression, sir.
Signior Baptista, you are happily met. / [To the Pedant] Sir, this is the gentleman I told you of; / I pray you stand good father to me now; / Give me Bianca for my patrimony.
Signior Baptista, how lucky to meet you. Sir, this is the gentleman I told you about. Please be a good father to me now. Give me Bianca in exchange for my inheritance.

Soft, son! / Sir, by your leave: having come to Padua / To gather in some debts, my son Lucentio / Made me acquainted with a weighty cause / Of love between your daughter and himself: / And,—for the good report I hear of you, / And for the love he beareth to your daughter, / And she to him,—to stay him not too long, / I am content, in a good father's care, / To have him match'd; and, if you please to like / No worse than I, upon some agreement / Me shall you find ready and willing / With one consent to have her so bestow'd; / For curious I cannot be with you, / Signior Baptista, of whom I hear so well.

Gently, son! Sir, with your permission: having come to Padua to collect some debts, my son Lucentio told me about a serious matter of love between your daughter and himself. And because of the good reports I hear of you, and because of the love he has for your daughter and she for him, so as not to keep him waiting too long, I'm happy, as a caring father, to see him married. And if you like it no less than I do, then once we reach some agreement you'll find me ready and willing to agree to her being matched with him. I can't be fussy with you, Signior Baptista, when I hear such good things of you.

Sir, pardon me in what I have to say. / Your plainness and your shortness please me well. / Right true it is your son Lucentio here / Doth love my daughter, and she loveth him, / Or both dissemble deeply their affections; / And therefore, if you say no more than this, / That like a father you will deal with him, / And pass my daughter a sufficient dower, / The match is made, and all is done: / Your son shall have my daughter with consent.

Sir, forgive me for what I have to say. Your frankness and brevity please me. It's quite true that your son Lucentio here loves my daughter, and she loves him, or else they're both very good at hiding their feelings. And so, if you'll say no more than this, that you'll treat him like a father and guarantee my daughter a sufficient settlement, the match is made and everything is done. Your son will have my daughter with my consent.
I thank you, sir. Where then do you know best / We be affied, and such assurance ta'en / As shall with either part's agreement stand?
Thank you, sir. Where do you think best for us to be formally engaged and have the guarantees drawn up that both parties will agree to?
Not in my house, Lucentio, for you know / Pitchers have ears, and I have many servants; / Besides, old Gremio is hearkening still, / And happily we might be interrupted.
Not in my house, Lucentio, because, you know, walls have ears, and I have many servants. Besides, old Gremio is always listening, and we might be interrupted.

Then at my lodging, and it like you: / There doth my father lie; and there this night / We'll pass the business privately and well. / Send for your daughter by your servant here; / My boy shall fetch the scrivener presently. / The worst is this, that at so slender warning / You are like to have a thin and slender pittance.

Then at my lodgings, if you like. My father is staying there, and tonight we'll settle the business privately and properly. Send for your daughter by your servant here. My boy will fetch the lawyer at once. The worst of it is that with such short notice you're likely to get a poor, meagre meal.

It likes me well. Cambio, hie you home, / And bid Bianca make her ready straight; / And, if you will, tell what hath happened: / Lucentio's father is arriv'd in Padua, / And how she's like to be Lucentio's wife.

That suits me. Cambio, hurry home and tell Bianca to get ready at once. And if you like, tell her what has happened: that Lucentio's father has arrived in Padua, and that she's likely to be Lucentio's wife.
I pray the gods she may, with all my heart!
I pray to the gods she will, with all my heart!
Dally not with the gods, but get thee gone. / Signior Baptista, shall I lead the way? / Welcome! One mess is like to be your cheer; / Come, sir; we will better it in Pisa.
Don't mess about with the gods; just get going. Signior Baptista, shall I lead the way? Welcome! One dish is likely to be your whole meal. Come, sir, we'll do better for you in Pisa.
You saw my master wink and laugh upon you?
Did you see my master wink and smile at you?
Faith, nothing; but has left me here behind to expound the meaning or / moral of his signs and tokens.
Honestly, nothing. But he's left me behind to explain the meaning, or moral, of his signs and signals.
Then thus: Baptista is safe, talking with the deceiving father of a / deceitful son.
Like this: Baptista is safely out of the way, talking with the fake father of a deceitful son.
His daughter is to be brought by you to the supper.
You're to bring his daughter to the supper.
The old priest at Saint Luke's church is at your command at all hours.
The old priest at Saint Luke's church is at your service at any hour.
And what does all this mean?

I cannot tell, except they are busied about a counterfeit assurance. / Take your assurance of her, cum privilegio ad imprimendum solum; to / the church! take the priest, clerk, and some sufficient honest / witnesses. If this be not that you look for, I have more to say, But / bid Bianca farewell for ever and a day.

I can't say, except that they're busy with a fake marriage settlement. You make your own settlement on her, with the sole right to print, as the books say. To the church! Take the priest, the clerk and some reliable, honest witnesses. If this isn't what you're looking for, I've nothing more to say, except: say goodbye to Bianca for ever and a day.

I cannot tarry: I knew a wench married in an afternoon as she went to / the garden for parsley to stuff a rabbit; and so may you, sir; and so / adieu, sir. My master hath appointed me to go to Saint Luke's to bid / the priest be ready to come against you come with your appendix.

I can't stay. I knew a girl who got married in an afternoon when she went to the garden to fetch parsley to stuff a rabbit, and so could you, sir. And so goodbye, sir. My master has told me to go to Saint Luke's and tell the priest to be ready for when you come with your appendage.
I may, and will, if she be so contented. / She will be pleas'd; then wherefore should I doubt? / Hap what hap may, I'll roundly go about her; / It shall go hard if Cambio go without her:
I can, and I will, if she agrees. She'll be pleased, so why should I doubt it? Whatever happens, I'll go straight at it with her. It'll be hard luck if Cambio goes without her.
Come on, i' God's name; once more toward our father's. / Good Lord, how bright and goodly shines the moon!
Come on, in God's name, once more towards our father's house. Good Lord, how bright and beautifully the moon is shining!
The moon! The sun; it is not moonlight now.
The moon! It's the sun. It isn't moonlight now.
I say it is the moon that shines so bright.
I say it's the moon that's shining so bright.
I know it is the sun that shines so bright.
I know it's the sun that's shining so bright.

Now by my mother's son, and that's myself, / It shall be moon, or star, or what I list, / Or ere I journey to your father's house. / Go on and fetch our horses back again. / Evermore cross'd and cross'd; nothing but cross'd!

Now, by my mother's son, and that's me, it will be the moon, or a star, or whatever I like, before I travel to your father's house. Go and bring our horses back again. Always contradicted, contradicted, nothing but contradicted!
Say as he says, or we shall never go.
Say what he says, or we'll never get there.
Forward, I pray, since we have come so far, / And be it moon, or sun, or what you please; / And if you please to call it a rush-candle, / Henceforth I vow it shall be so for me.
Go on, please, since we've come so far, and let it be the moon, or the sun, or whatever you like. And if you choose to call it a cheap candle, I swear from now on it will be one for me.
I say it is the moon.
I know it is the moon.
Nay, then you lie; it is the blessed sun.
No, then you're lying. It's the blessed sun.

Then, God be bless'd, it is the blessed sun; / But sun it is not when you say it is not, / And the moon changes even as your mind. / What you will have it nam'd, even that it is, / And so it shall be so for Katherine.

Then, God be blessed, it's the blessed sun. But it isn't the sun when you say it isn't, and the moon changes just like your mind. Whatever you want it called, that's what it is, and that's what it will be for Katherine.
Petruchio, go thy ways; the field is won.
Petruchio, carry on. The battle is won.
Well, forward, forward! thus the bowl should run, / And not unluckily against the bias. / But, soft! Company is coming here.
Well, onward, onward! This is how the bowl should run, and not perversely against its natural curve. But wait! Someone's coming.

[To Vincentio] Good morrow, gentle mistress; where away? / Tell me, sweet Kate, and tell me truly too, / Hast thou beheld a fresher gentlewoman? / Such war of white and red within her cheeks! / What stars do spangle heaven with such beauty / As those two eyes become that heavenly face? / Fair lovely maid, once more good day to thee. / Sweet Kate, embrace her for her beauty's sake.

Good morning, gentle lady. Where are you going? Tell me, sweet Kate, and tell me honestly, have you ever seen a fresher young lady? Such a battle of white and red in her cheeks! What stars light up the sky as beautifully as those two eyes suit that heavenly face? Beautiful, lovely girl, once more good day to you. Sweet Kate, embrace her for her beauty's sake.
A will make the man mad, to make a woman of him.
He'll drive the man mad, making a woman of him.

Young budding virgin, fair and fresh and sweet, / Whither away, or where is thy abode? / Happy the parents of so fair a child; / Happier the man whom favourable stars / Allot thee for his lovely bedfellow.

Young, budding girl, fair and fresh and sweet, where are you going, and where do you live? Happy are the parents of so lovely a child, and happier the man whom kind stars give you to as his lovely bedfellow.
Why, how now, Kate! I hope thou art not mad: / This is a man, old, wrinkled, faded, wither'd, / And not a maiden, as thou sayst he is.
Why, what's this, Kate? I hope you're not mad. This is a man: old, wrinkled, faded and withered, not a girl, as you say he is.

Pardon, old father, my mistaking eyes, / That have been so bedazzled with the sun / That everything I look on seemeth green: / Now I perceive thou art a reverend father; / Pardon, I pray thee, for my mad mistaking.
Forgive my mistaken eyes, old father. They've been so dazzled by the sun that everything I look at seems green and young. Now I see you're a respected old man. Please forgive me for my mad mistake.
Do, good old grandsire, and withal make known / Which way thou travellest: if along with us, / We shall be joyful of thy company.
Do forgive her, good old grandfather, and tell us which way you're travelling. If it's our way, we'll be glad of your company.

Fair sir, and you my merry mistress, / That with your strange encounter much amaz'd me, / My name is called Vincentio; my dwelling Pisa; / And bound I am to Padua, there to visit / A son of mine, which long I have not seen.

Good sir, and you, my merry lady, who astonished me with your strange greeting: my name is Vincentio, I live in Pisa, and I'm on my way to Padua to visit a son of mine whom I haven't seen for a long time.

Happily met; the happier for thy son. / And now by law, as well as reverend age, / I may entitle thee my loving father: / The sister to my wife, this gentlewoman, / Thy son by this hath married. Wonder not, / Nor be not griev'd: she is of good esteem, / Her dowry wealthy, and of worthy birth; / Beside, so qualified as may beseem / The spouse of any noble gentleman. / Let me embrace with old Vincentio; / And wander we to see thy honest son, / Who will of thy arrival be full joyous.

Happily met, and happier for your son. And now by law, as well as by your respected age, I can call you my loving father. Your son has by now married this lady's sister, my wife's sister. Don't be surprised or upset: she has a good reputation, a rich dowry and good birth, and besides, she has all the qualities fit for the wife of any noble gentleman. Let me embrace old Vincentio, and let's travel on to see your honest son, who'll be overjoyed at your arrival.
But is this true? or is it else your pleasure, / Like pleasant travellers, to break a jest / Upon the company you overtake?
But is this true? Or are you just enjoying yourself, like playful travellers, by playing a joke on the people you meet on the road?
I do assure thee, father, so it is.
I assure you, father, it's true.
Come, go along, and see the truth hereof; / For our first merriment hath made thee jealous.
Come along and see the truth of it for yourself, because our first joke has made you suspicious.
Well, Petruchio, this has put me in heart. / Have to my widow! and if she be froward, / Then hast thou taught Hortensio to be untoward.
Well, Petruchio, this has given me heart. Off to my widow! And if she's stubborn, then you've taught Hortensio to be rough.
Softly and swiftly, sir, for the priest is ready.
Quietly and quickly, sir, because the priest is ready.
I fly, Biondello; but they may chance to need thee at home, therefore / leave us.
I'm flying, Biondello. But they might need you at home, so leave us.
Nay, faith, I'll see the church o' your back; and then come back to my / master's as soon as I can.
No, honestly, I'll see the church at your back, and then come back to my master's as soon as I can.
I marvel Cambio comes not all this while.
I'm surprised Cambio hasn't come all this time.
Sir, here's the door; this is Lucentio's house: / My father's bears more toward the market-place; / Thither must I, and here I leave you, sir.
Sir, here's the door. This is Lucentio's house. My father-in-law's is nearer the market square. I must go there, and here I'll leave you, sir.
You shall not choose but drink before you go. / I think I shall command your welcome here, / And by all likelihood some cheer is toward.
You must have a drink before you go. I think I can make you welcome here, and very likely there's some celebration going on.
They're busy within; you were best knock louder.
They're busy inside. You'd better knock louder.
What's he that knocks as he would beat down the gate?
Who's that knocking as if he wants to beat down the door?
He's within, sir, but not to be spoken withal.
He's in, sir, but he can't be spoken to.
What if a man bring him a hundred pound or two to make merry withal?
What if someone brings him a hundred pounds or two to enjoy himself with?
Keep your hundred pounds to yourself: he shall need none so long as I / live.
Keep your hundred pounds to yourself. He won't need any as long as I'm alive.

Nay, I told you your son was well beloved in Padua. Do you hear, sir? / To leave frivolous circumstances, I pray you tell Signior Lucentio that / his father is come from Pisa, and is here at the door to speak with / him.

There, I told you your son was well loved in Padua. Do you hear, sir? Leaving aside all this nonsense, please tell Signior Lucentio that his father has come from Pisa and is here at the door to speak to him.
Thou liest: his father is come from Padua, and here looking out at the / window.
You're lying. His father has come from Padua, and is here looking out of the window.
Ay, sir; so his mother says, if I may believe her.
Yes, sir, so his mother says, if I can believe her.
[To Vincentio] Why, how now, gentleman! why, this is flat knavery to / take upon you another man's name.
Why, what's this, sir? Why, it's downright fraud to take another man's name.
Lay hands on the villain: I believe a means to cozen somebody in this / city under my countenance.
Seize the villain. I believe he means to cheat somebody in this city by pretending to be me.
I have seen them in the church together: God send 'em good shipping! / But who is here? Mine old master, Vincentio! Now we are undone and / brought to nothing.
I've seen them in the church together. God send them a good voyage! But who's this? My old master, Vincentio! Now we're ruined and done for.
I hope I may choose, sir.
I hope I can do as I like, sir.
Come hither, you rogue. What, have you forgot me?
Come here, you rogue. What, have you forgotten me?
Forgot you! No, sir: I could not forget you, for I never saw you before / in all my life.
Forgotten you! No, sir. I couldn't forget you, because I've never seen you before in my life.
What, you notorious villain! didst thou never see thy master's father, / Vincentio?
What, you notorious villain! Have you never seen your master's father, Vincentio?
What, my old worshipful old master? Yes, marry, sir; see where he looks / out of the window.
What, my old, honoured old master? Yes, indeed, sir. Look, there he is, looking out of the window.
Help, help, help! here's a madman will murder me.
Help, help, help! Here's a madman who'll murder me.
Prithee, Kate, let's stand aside and see the end of this controversy.
Please, Kate, let's stand aside and see how this argument ends.
Sir, what are you that offer to beat my servant?
Sir, who are you to try to beat my servant?

What am I, sir! nay, what are you, sir? O immortal gods! O fine / villain! A silken doublet, a velvet hose, a scarlet cloak, and a / copatain hat! O, I am undone! I am undone! While I play the good / husband at home, my son and my servant spend all at the university.

Who am I, sir? No, who are you, sir? Oh immortal gods! Oh, you fine villain! A silk jacket, velvet breeches, a scarlet cloak and a tall pointed hat! Oh, I'm ruined! I'm ruined! While I'm being careful with money at home, my son and my servant are spending it all at the university.
Sir, you seem a sober ancient gentleman by your habit, but your words / show you a madman. Why, sir, what 'cerns it you if I wear pearl and / gold? I thank my good father, I am able to maintain it.
Sir, from your clothes you look like a sensible old gentleman, but your words show you're a madman. Why, sir, what's it to you if I wear pearls and gold? Thanks to my good father, I can afford it.
Thy father! O villain! he is a sailmaker in Bergamo.
Your father! Oh, you villain! He's a sailmaker in Bergamo.
You mistake, sir; you mistake, sir. Pray, what do you think is his / name?
You're mistaken, sir, you're mistaken, sir. Please, what do you think his name is?
His name! As if I knew not his name! I have brought him up ever since / he was three years old, and his name is Tranio.
His name! As if I didn't know his name! I've brought him up since he was three years old, and his name is Tranio.
Away, away, mad ass! His name is Lucentio; and he is mine only son, and / heir to the lands of me, Signior Vincentio.
Get away, get away, you mad ass! His name is Lucentio, and he's my only son and heir to my lands, mine, Signior Vincentio's.
Lucentio! O, he hath murdered his master! Lay hold on him, I charge / you, in the Duke's name. O, my son, my son! Tell me, thou villain, / where is my son, Lucentio?
Lucentio! Oh, he has murdered his master! Seize him, I order you, in the Duke's name. Oh, my son, my son! Tell me, you villain, where is my son Lucentio?
Carry this mad knave to the gaol. Father Baptista, I charge you see / that he be forthcoming.
Take this mad rascal to prison. Father Baptista, I ask you to make sure he's kept for trial.
Stay, officer; he shall not go to prison.
Wait, officer. He won't go to prison.
Talk not, Signior Gremio; I say he shall go to prison.
Don't interfere, Signior Gremio. I say he will go to prison.
Take heed, Signior Baptista, lest you be cony-catched in this business; / I dare swear this is the right Vincentio.
Be careful, Signior Baptista, that you're not swindled in this business. I'd swear this is the real Vincentio.
Nay, I dare not swear it.
No, I don't dare swear it.
Then thou wert best say that I am not Lucentio.
Then you'd better say I'm not Lucentio.
Yes, I know thee to be Signior Lucentio.
Yes, I know you're Signior Lucentio.
Away with the dotard! to the gaol with him!
Away with the old fool! To prison with him!
Thus strangers may be haled and abus'd: O monstrous villain!
So strangers can be dragged off and mistreated. Oh, monstrous villain!
O! we are spoiled; and yonder he is: deny him, forswear him, or else we / are all undone.
Oh, we're ruined, and there he is! Deny him, disown him, or we're all done for.
How hast thou offended? / Where is Lucentio?
What have you done wrong? Where is Lucentio?
Here's Lucentio, / Right son to the right Vincentio; / That have by marriage made thy daughter mine, / While counterfeit supposes blear'd thine eyne.
Here's Lucentio, true son of the true Vincentio, who has made your daughter mine by marriage while fake impostors blinded your eyes.
Here 's packing, with a witness, to deceive us all!
Here's a conspiracy, and no mistake, to deceive us all!
Where is that damned villain, Tranio, / That fac'd and brav'd me in this matter so?
Where's that damned villain Tranio, who defied and insulted me to my face in this business?
Why, tell me, is not this my Cambio?
Why, tell me, isn't this my Cambio?

Love wrought these miracles. Bianca's love / Made me exchange my state with Tranio, / While he did bear my countenance in the town; / And happily I have arriv'd at the last / Unto the wished haven of my bliss. / What Tranio did, myself enforc'd him to; / Then pardon him, sweet father, for my sake.

Love worked these miracles. Love for Bianca made me exchange places with Tranio while he played me in the town, and happily I have at last reached the harbour of happiness I wished for. What Tranio did, I made him do, so forgive him, dear father, for my sake.
I'll slit the villain's nose that would have sent me to the gaol.
I'll slit the nose of the villain who would have sent me to prison.
[To Lucentio] But do you hear, sir? Have you married my daughter / without asking my good will?
But listen, sir: have you married my daughter without asking my permission?
Fear not, Baptista; we will content you, go to: but I will in, to be / revenged for this villainy.
Don't worry, Baptista. We'll satisfy you, come on. But I'll go in and get my revenge for this villainy.
And I to sound the depth of this knavery.
And I'll go and get to the bottom of this trickery.
Look not pale, Bianca; thy father will not frown.
Don't look pale, Bianca. Your father won't stay angry.
My cake is dough, but I'll in among the rest; / Out of hope of all but my share of the feast.
My cake is dough: I've failed. But I'll go in with the rest, hoping for nothing but my share of the feast.
Husband, let's follow to see the end of this ado.
Husband, let's follow and see how all this fuss ends.
First kiss me, Kate, and we will.
Kiss me first, Kate, and we will.
What! in the midst of the street?
What! In the middle of the street?
What! art thou ashamed of me?
What! Are you ashamed of me?
No, sir; God forbid; but ashamed to kiss.
No, sir, God forbid, but ashamed to kiss.
Why, then, let's home again. Come, sirrah, let's away.
Why, then, let's go home again. Come on, you, let's go.
Nay, I will give thee a kiss: now pray thee, love, stay.
No, I'll give you a kiss. Now please, love, stay.
Is not this well? Come, my sweet Kate: / Better once than never, for never too late.
Isn't this good? Come, my sweet Kate. Better once than never, because it's never too late.

At last, though long, our jarring notes agree: / And time it is when raging war is done, / To smile at 'scapes and perils overblown. / My fair Bianca, bid my father welcome, / While I with self-same kindness welcome thine. / Brother Petruchio, sister Katherina, / And thou, Hortensio, with thy loving widow, / Feast with the best, and welcome to my house: / My banquet is to close our stomachs up, / After our great good cheer. Pray you, sit down; / For now we sit to chat as well as eat.

At last, after a long time, our clashing notes are in harmony, and now that the raging war is over, it's time to smile at narrow escapes and dangers that have passed. My lovely Bianca, welcome my father, while I welcome yours with the same kindness. Brother Petruchio, sister Katherina, and you, Hortensio, with your loving widow, enjoy the best food, and welcome to my house. This banquet is a dessert to round off our great feast. Please sit down, because now we're sitting to chat as well as to eat.
Nothing but sit and sit, and eat and eat!
Nothing but sitting and sitting, and eating and eating!
Padua affords this kindness, son Petruchio.
Padua offers this kindness, son Petruchio.
Padua affords nothing but what is kind.
Padua offers nothing that isn't kind.
For both our sakes I would that word were true.
For both our sakes, I wish that were true.
Now, for my life, Hortensio fears his widow.
Now, on my life, Hortensio is afraid of his widow.
Then never trust me if I be afeard.
Then never trust me if I'm afraid.
You are very sensible, and yet you miss my sense: / I mean Hortensio is afeard of you.
You're very sensible, and yet you miss my sense. I mean Hortensio is afraid of you.
He that is giddy thinks the world turns round.
Someone who's dizzy thinks the world is spinning round.
Madam, what do you mean by that?
That's what I gather from him.
Conceives by me! How likes Hortensio that?
Conceive by me! How does Hortensio like that?
My widow says thus she conceives her tale.
My widow means that's how she understands his remark.
Very well mended. Kiss him for that, good widow.
Very well rescued. Kiss him for that, good widow.
'He that is giddy thinks the world turns round': / I pray you tell me what you meant by that.
"Someone who's dizzy thinks the world is spinning round." Please tell me what you meant by that.
Your husband, being troubled with a shrew, / Measures my husband's sorrow by his woe; / And now you know my meaning.
Your husband, being troubled with a shrew, judges my husband's sorrow by his own misery. And now you know my meaning.
And I am mean, indeed, respecting you.
And I'm being mild, indeed, compared with you.
A hundred marks, my Kate does put her down.
A hundred marks says my Kate will floor her.
Spoke like an officer: ha' to thee, lad.
Spoken like a man on duty. Here's to you, lad.
How likes Gremio these quick-witted folks?
How does Gremio like these quick-witted people?
Believe me, sir, they butt together well.
Believe me, sir, they butt heads well together.
Head and butt! An hasty-witted body / Would say your head and butt were head and horn.
Head and butt! A quick-witted person would say your head and butt were a head and a horn.
Ay, mistress bride, hath that awaken'd you?
Yes, madam bride, has that woken you up?
Ay, but not frighted me; therefore I'll sleep again.
Yes, but it hasn't frightened me, so I'll go back to sleep.
Nay, that you shall not; since you have begun, / Have at you for a bitter jest or two.
No, you won't. Since you've started, I'll have a go at you with a sharp joke or two.
Am I your bird? I mean to shift my bush, / And then pursue me as you draw your bow. / You are welcome all.
Am I your bird? I mean to move to another bush, and then you can chase me while you draw your bow. You're all welcome.
She hath prevented me. Here, Signior Tranio; / This bird you aim'd at, though you hit her not: / Therefore a health to all that shot and miss'd.
She's got away from me. Here, Signior Tranio: this is the bird you aimed at, though you didn't hit her. So here's a toast to everyone who shot and missed.
O, sir! Lucentio slipp'd me like his greyhound, / Which runs himself, and catches for his master.
Oh, sir, Lucentio let me off the leash like his greyhound, which runs for itself and catches for its master.
A good swift simile, but something currish.
A good quick comparison, but a bit doggy.
'Tis well, sir, that you hunted for yourself: / 'Tis thought your deer does hold you at a bay.
It's a good thing, sir, that you hunted for yourself. People think your deer is keeping you at bay.
O ho, Petruchio! Tranio hits you now.
Oh ho, Petruchio! Tranio has hit you now.
I thank thee for that gird, good Tranio.
Thank you for that dig, good Tranio.
Confess, confess; hath he not hit you here?
Admit it, admit it. Hasn't he hit you there?
A has a little gall'd me, I confess; / And as the jest did glance away from me, / 'Tis ten to one it maim'd you two outright.
He's stung me a little, I admit. And as the joke glanced off me, it's ten to one it wounded you two badly.
Now, in good sadness, son Petruchio, / I think thou hast the veriest shrew of all.
Now, in all seriousness, son Petruchio, I think you've got the worst shrew of all.

Well, I say no; and therefore, for assurance, / Let's each one send unto his wife, / And he whose wife is most obedient, / To come at first when he doth send for her, / Shall win the wager which we will propose.
Well, I say no. And so, to prove it, let's each send for his wife, and the man whose wife is most obedient, and comes first when he sends for her, will win the bet we're going to make.
Twenty crowns! / I'll venture so much of my hawk or hound, / But twenty times so much upon my wife.
Twenty crowns! I'd bet that much on my hawk or hound, but twenty times as much on my wife.
That will I. / Go, Biondello, bid your mistress come to me.
I will. Go, Biondello, and tell your mistress to come to me.
Son, I'll be your half, Bianca comes.
Son, I'll go halves with you that Bianca comes.
I'll have no halves; I'll bear it all myself.
I won't have halves. I'll take it all on myself.
Sir, my mistress sends you word / That she is busy and she cannot come.
Sir, my mistress sends you word that she's busy and can't come.
How! She's busy, and she cannot come! / Is that an answer?
What! She's busy and can't come! Is that an answer?
Ay, and a kind one too: / Pray God, sir, your wife send you not a worse.
Yes, and a kind one too. Pray God, sir, your wife doesn't send you a worse one.
Sirrah Biondello, go and entreat my wife / To come to me forthwith.
Biondello, go and ask my wife politely to come to me at once.
O, ho! entreat her! / Nay, then she must needs come.
Oh ho! Ask her politely! No, then she's bound to come.
I am afraid, sir, / Do what you can, yours will not be entreated.
I'm afraid, sir, whatever you do, yours won't be persuaded.
She says you have some goodly jest in hand: / She will not come; she bids you come to her.
She says you have some fine joke going on. She won't come. She tells you to come to her.
Worse and worse; she will not come! O vile, / Intolerable, not to be endur'd! / Sirrah Grumio, go to your mistress, / Say I command her come to me.
Worse and worse. She won't come! Oh, vile, intolerable, not to be put up with! Grumio, go to your mistress and say I order her to come to me.
The fouler fortune mine, and there an end.
Then it's my bad luck, and that's the end of it.
Now, by my holidame, here comes Katherina!
Now, by Our Lady, here comes Katherina!
What is your will sir, that you send for me?
What do you want, sir, that you've sent for me?
Where is your sister, and Hortensio's wife?
Where's your sister, and Hortensio's wife?
They sit conferring by the parlour fire.
They're sitting chatting by the parlour fire.
Go fetch them hither; if they deny to come, / Swinge me them soundly forth unto their husbands. / Away, I say, and bring them hither straight.
Go and fetch them here. If they refuse to come, give them a good beating and drive them out to their husbands. Go, I tell you, and bring them here at once.
Here is a wonder, if you talk of a wonder.
Here's a wonder, if you want to talk about wonders.
And so it is. I wonder what it bodes.
So it is. I wonder what it means.
Marry, peace it bodes, and love, and quiet life, / An awful rule, and right supremacy; / And, to be short, what not that's sweet and happy.
Why, it means peace, and love, and a quiet life, rule that commands respect and proper authority. In short, everything that's sweet and happy.

Now fair befall thee, good Petruchio! / The wager thou hast won; and I will add / Unto their losses twenty thousand crowns; / Another dowry to another daughter, / For she is chang'd, as she had never been.

Now good luck to you, good Petruchio! You've won the bet, and I'll add twenty thousand crowns to their losses: another dowry for another daughter, because she's changed as if she'd never been the same person.

Nay, I will win my wager better yet, / And show more sign of her obedience, / Her new-built virtue and obedience. / See where she comes, and brings your froward wives / As prisoners to her womanly persuasion.

No, I'll win my bet even more clearly, and show more evidence of her obedience, her newly built virtue and obedience. Look, here she comes, bringing your stubborn wives as prisoners of her womanly persuasion.
Katherine, that cap of yours becomes you not: / Off with that bauble, throw it underfoot.
Katherine, that cap doesn't suit you. Take that trinket off and throw it under your foot.
Lord, let me never have a cause to sigh / Till I be brought to such a silly pass!
Lord, never let me have reason to sigh until I'm brought to such a silly state!
Fie! what a foolish duty call you this?
Shame! What kind of foolish duty do you call this?
I would your duty were as foolish too; / The wisdom of your duty, fair Bianca, / Hath cost me a hundred crowns since supper-time!
I wish your duty were as foolish too. The wisdom of your duty, lovely Bianca, has cost me a hundred crowns since supper!
The more fool you for laying on my duty.
The more fool you for betting on my duty.
Katherine, I charge thee, tell these headstrong women / What duty they do owe their lords and husbands.
Katherine, I order you, tell these headstrong women what duty they owe their lords and husbands.
Come, come, you're mocking; we will have no telling.
Come on, come on, you're mocking us. We won't have any lecture.
Come on, I say; and first begin with her.
Go on, I tell you, and start with her.
I say she shall: and first begin with her.
I say she will. And start with her.

Fie, fie! unknit that threatening unkind brow, / And dart not scornful glances from those eyes / To wound thy lord, thy king, thy governor: / It blots thy beauty as frosts do bite the meads, / Confounds thy fame as whirlwinds shake fair buds, / And in no sense is meet or amiable. / A woman mov'd is like a fountain troubled, / Muddy, ill-seeming, thick, bereft of beauty; / And while it is so, none so dry or thirsty / Will deign to sip or touch one drop of it. / Thy husband is thy lord, thy life, thy keeper, / Thy head, thy sovereign; one that cares for thee, / And for thy maintenance commits his body / To painful labour both by sea and land, / To watch the night in storms, the day in cold, / Whilst thou liest warm at home, secure and safe; / And craves no other tribute at thy hands / But love, fair looks, and true obedience; / Too little payment for so great a debt. / Such duty as the subject owes the prince, / Even such a woman oweth to her husband; / And when she is froward, peevish, sullen, sour, / And not obedient to his honest will, / What is she but a foul contending rebel / And graceless traitor to her loving lord?— / I am asham'd that women are so simple / To offer war where they should kneel for peace, / Or seek for rule, supremacy, and sway, / When they are bound to serve, love, and obey. / Why are our bodies soft and weak and smooth, / Unapt to toil and trouble in the world, / But that our soft conditions and our hearts / Should well agree with our external parts? / Come, come, you froward and unable worms! / My mind hath been as big as one of yours, / My heart as great, my reason haply more, / To bandy word for word and frown for frown; / But now I see our lances are but straws, / Our strength as weak, our weakness past compare, / That seeming to be most which we indeed least are. / Then vail your stomachs, for it is no boot, / And place your hands below your husband's foot: / In token of which duty, if he please, / My hand is ready; may it do him ease.

Shame, shame! Smooth out that threatening, unkind frown, and don't dart scornful looks from those eyes to wound your lord, your king, your governor. It spoils your beauty as frost nips the meadows, ruins your reputation as whirlwinds shake lovely buds, and is in no way fitting or attractive. An angry woman is like a fountain that has been stirred up: muddy, ugly, thick, robbed of its beauty. And while it's like that, nobody, however dry or thirsty, will stoop to sip or touch a drop of it. Your husband is your lord, your life, your keeper, your head, your sovereign: someone who cares for you, and to support you puts his body through hard work on sea and land, staying awake at night in storms and by day in the cold, while you lie warm at home, safe and secure. And he asks no other payment from you but love, kind looks and true obedience: too little payment for so great a debt. The same duty a subject owes his ruler, a woman owes her husband. And when she's stubborn, irritable, sulky, sour, and doesn't obey his honest wishes, what is she but a vile, quarrelling rebel and a wicked traitor to her loving lord? I'm ashamed that women are so foolish as to declare war when they should kneel for peace, or seek to rule, dominate and control, when they're bound to serve, love and obey. Why are our bodies soft and weak and smooth, unfit for hard work and trouble in the world, unless it's so that our gentle natures and our hearts should match our outward parts? Come, come, you stubborn, feeble worms! My spirit has been as proud as either of yours, my heart as great, my reason perhaps greater, to trade word for word and frown for frown. But now I see our lances are only straws, our strength as weak as straw, our weakness beyond compare, so that we seem to be most what in fact we are least. So lower your pride, because it's no use, and place your hands beneath your husband's foot. As a sign of that duty, if he wishes, my hand is ready. May it give him pleasure.
Why, there's a wench! Come on, and kiss me, Kate.
Why, there's a girl! Come on and kiss me, Kate.
Well, go thy ways, old lad, for thou shalt ha't.
Well, good for you, old lad, because you've won it.
'Tis a good hearing when children are toward.
It's good to hear when children are obedient.
But a harsh hearing when women are froward.
But hard to hear when women are stubborn.
Come, Kate, we'll to bed. / We three are married, but you two are sped. / 'Twas I won the wager, / [To Lucentio] though you hit the white; / And being a winner, God give you good night!
Come, Kate, we'll go to bed. Three of us are married, but you two are done for. It was I who won the bet, though you hit the bullseye. And as the winner, God give you good night!
Now go thy ways; thou hast tam'd a curst shrew.
Well, good for you. You've tamed a cursed shrew.
'Tis a wonder, by your leave, she will be tam'd so.
It's a wonder, if you'll pardon me saying so, that she lets herself be tamed like this.
